news.title: Who’s Left?
news.text:
Republicans and pundits will play the “blame game” for a while and try to analyze “what happened” on Tuesday, November 3. And perhaps we can learn something (I doubt it). But I’m not going to do that in this article (although I just did it in a video podcast on my Substack). Tuesday’s done; it’s over, and we can’t change the results. We can try to learn from it (again, we probably won’t), pick up the pieces, and try to make sure it never happens again. And, well, it’s not like it’s never happened before. The Republicans lost 41 seats in the House in 2018, though, interestingly, they actually gained two seats in the Senate. 2026, obviously, is much worse.

So, pick up the pieces. What’s left? Frankly, not much. I’m not sure Texas is totally gone, like California and New York are, but if so, that would be very damaging. Florida is now the main Republican bulwark. What else? Well, Alabama, Louisiana, Arkansas, and Oklahoma are still pretty solid (Mississippi not so much so; Georgia is gone); Tennessee and West Virginia are still strongly Republican (I have worries about Kentucky’s inconsistency), and then there are Wyoming, Idaho, and Utah that are very dependable, with maybe Montana and the Dakotas. Indiana can usually be counted on, and Missouri, too.

And that’s just about it. Republicans have about 10 “solids” and a few “usuallys.” Fifteen or so out of 50. Alaska and Mississippi may go for Democratic senators this year (it’s still undecided at this writing), but any state that repeatedly elects Lisa Murkowski as senator (Alaska) isn’t to be trusted anyway. There’s just not much left, folks, and except for Florida, the populations of all the rest of those states combined aren’t much more than California’s. Only Tennessee ranks in the top 15 in state population. In fact, let me list the top 15 states in population:

1. California: 39,355,309

2. Texas: 31,709,821

3. Florida: 23,462,518

4. New York: 20,002,427

5. Pennsylvania: 13,059,432

6. Illinois: 12,719,141

7. Ohio: 11,900,510

8. Georgia: 11,302,748

9. North Carolina: 11,197,968

10. Michigan: 10,127,884

11. New Jersey: 9,548,215

12. Virginia: 8,880,107

13. Washington: 8,001,020

14. Arizona: 7,623,818

15. Tennessee: 7,315,076

That is not a long list of states that voted Republican this year, or generally do so, and pardon my sarcasm. Yes, Mr. Trump won several of them in 2016 and 2024, but we mustn’t overlook who Trump defeated — Hillary Clinton and Kamala Harris. If you can find me two more…unattractive, unappealing, unpleasant, distasteful women in the United States than those two, I’d like to know who they are (they do have some competition, I admit). So, did the American people really find Donald Trump so overwhelmingly appealing that they gave him victories, or was he greatly assisted by Democratic Party stupidity?

Well, be that as it may, my point here is that only two of the top 15 states in population are reliably Republican, and one of those is number 15. And of the Western states that are “reliably” Republican, only Utah has a population over three million. Many Democratic hellhole urban areas have more people than most of the western states. Demographics are not with the Republicans here, not for the foreseeable future.

And even when the Republicans win the House of Representatives now, they get the barest of majorities and a weak Speaker. Democrats are going to have well over 250 seats in the House this term with a belligerent Speaker who hates Republicans and America. The Republicans did have 53 Senate seats the past two years; the Democrats will have at least 54 this time (two are still undecided, and right now the votes are being led by Democrats). And, of course, add several RINOs to the Democratic number. There are no “DINOs” on the Democratic Party side of the aisle. It’s not pretty.

I’m not trying to be pessimistic here; I’m just trying to be realistic. We don’t have many reliable states left, while the Democrats have many they can always count on, and those are most of the largest states in the Union. Republicans need to be trying to build some new coalitions, but…who? Unfortunately, America is moving leftward toward dependence and decadence, and those two qualities are tailor-made for Democrats.

Righteous nations do not fall; the people in such a country have the qualities and characteristics necessary to remain spiritually, morally, and nationally strong. While never perfect, America became a great nation because its people were largely spiritually and morally united. When decadence sets in, a nation begins to decline and ultimately collapse. And it’s happening rapidly in America now.

America, today, can in no shape, form, or fashion be called a “righteous” nation anymore. There are still good, godly people in the country, of course, but they are far in the minority now. No nation that lets its babies be murdered in the womb, that butchers its children for sexual purposes, that exalts sexual immorality and perversion, that doesn’t know the difference between a man and a woman, or what marriage and a family are anymore, that opens its borders and lets criminals walk the streets with impunity…no nation that allows and tolerates those things, much less has its majority political party supporting them, can be called “righteous.” Decadent, yes. Righteous, no.

When God is removed from the human spirit, the only thing that remains is an animal and a jungle. Like what America has become in too many places now, and like America elected in so many places on Tuesday. The dominance of evil human hearts is the supreme problem America now faces — in the streets and in government — and that is a problem that is exceedingly difficult to solve. How do you change the human heart?

So, after Tuesday, who’s left? Not very many, I’m afraid. But that doesn’t mean we quit fighting; it only means we fight harder.

My Substacks are a little unique. Not just current events, but history, our Founding Fathers, what America was meant to be, and Biblical exegesis. Check them out. “Mark It Down! (mklewis929.substack.com) and “Mark It Down! Bible Substack” (mklbibless.substack.com) Both free. Follow me on X: @thailandmkl. Read my western novels, "Whitewater," "River Bend," "Return to River Bend," "Allie’s Dilemma," and "Kendrick," all available on Amazon.

news.title: Crossing a Cred Line
news.text:
When leaving such a movie, one doesn’t feel that he is morally confused to like the vigilante and loathe the bad guys whom he killed. Okay, okay, it’s only a movie, but like a Rorschach Test, how we respond can say a good deal about who we are.

If you can’t condemn Hamas and its actions, then you are morally perverse.

Hitler and his modern “Woke Right” acolytes understood that the Jew had to be completely demonized. He and they could not afford a system in which a normal person looks at a child who has done no wrong or a neighbor who has always been there for him and then starts to use his brain to get to a rational conclusion that these people don’t deserve to suffer or die. Hermann Göring bellowed that 60 million Germans tell him that the Jews are swine, but there is this one single Jew whom he knows, and the guy is A-Okay. What the Left in the West, hand-in-hand with the Qatari-funded Muslim Brotherhood, wish to do is to make first Israel and then later Jews so evil in the world’s thinking that doing anything to them would be considered to be the right thing to do. It took the U.N. eons to actually admit that Hamas engaged in a clearly recognizable pattern of sexual violence. Heck, its guys came with instructions on how to say in Hebrew to get undressed, etc. The U.N. could not condemn Hamas, because its own UNRWA made the attack possible. Vice President JD Vance made it his business to blame the Iran War and Israel’s relationship with the U.S. as major contributors to the Republican wipeout this week. No, it wasn’t the high cost of living or the lack of affordable housing for many young Americans. The Iran War could have ended months ago, with gas going down to under $3 a gallon if Vance had not played lawyer for Qatar and Pakistan with his MOU and wasted negotiations. As to Israel, Secretary of War Pete Hegseth and Secretary of State Marco Rubio understand that she is a great ally of the U.S. I know living here how much Israelis love the U.S. and appreciate her support and friendship. The only ones making the Israel is bad for the U.S. argument are Jew-hating Muslims, lefties who see Jews as oppressors, and losers on the right like JD’s bestest buddy, Tucker Carlson. Israel did not cause the Republicans to lose. As in all U.S. elections since time immemorial, Americans voted with their pocketbook and found it missing a lot of cash. Much of the damage was done under Biden, but tariffs and dragging out the war did not help to make things better. I believe that Donald Trump’s economy will improve until he leaves office. But people voted on Tuesday based on how they felt economically on Monday.

With Vance’s Israel-hatred (which is always Jew hatred with a few cheap garments over it) so clear, I am left in a bit of a pickle. I cannot and will not write to help an antisemite become president of the United States. Even if JD Vance felt what he said was true, he could have used some of his brain (I know, he went to Yale, so this is a bit of a stretch) to realize that now is not the moment to criticize Israel. But I also cannot write to further rip apart the frayed and still fraying “Republican coalition.” Thus, for the good of all, I will be signing off for some time.

I have enjoyed writing for Townhall, and the staff here has been both professional and extremely friendly. Townhall is an amazing website, as are its readers, whose comments and support I have enjoyed. Some of the best in the business write on this website, and I will continue to read their work and keep up my subscription. I cannot help JD get elected, and I will not sit around and attack the guy who may be the next Republican candidate for president. Donald Trump was truly a one-off. There are many great people in his orbit. JD Vance is not one of them.

news.title: The MAGA Movement Forgot What Populism Is
news.text:
Tuesday's election wasn't a blue wave or even a blue tsunami: It was a blue apocalypse.

Gov. Ron DeSantis (R-FL), who leads the one notable bright spot on the map, referred to the wipeout as "close to an extinction-level event" for the GOP. It was the worst midterm defeat for one party in over a half-century.

Much of the postmortem conversation has focused on why this massacre happened. Was it the Iran war? Was it the tariffs? Was it corruption? Was it the "Epstein files" mess?

The answer is both simpler and more sweeping: The MAGA movement, which has defined the GOP during the Trump era, has forgotten what populism means in practice and requires in governance.

When Donald Trump rode down the Trump Tower escalator in 2015, he launched a populist revolution. His message was simple: An elite ruling class has sold out the country, and the MAGA movement is here to finally listen to the people.

Trump largely delivered during his first term.

Trump cut taxes, tamed inflation, and oversaw a booming job market and a surging stock market. He became the first president since Richard Nixon to begin to reset our relationship with communist China.

In exile during the Joe Biden interregnum, Trump promised to return and close the border, get inflation under control, and bring back general sanity and stability.

To be sure, Trump's second term has had its successes.

The southern border is airtight. Violent crime has fallen to the lowest rate in 125 years. Prescription drug prices are the lowest since the 1960s. The Justice Department's fights with the Ivy League yielded real concessions. The raid to extract Nicolas Maduro from Caracas was bold and masterful.

But somewhere along the way, the MAGA movement forgot what it was.

Some in and around the administration have engaged in the most brazen corruption — pardons, access, illicit cryptocurrency enrichment, real estate side deals — in a century or more of Washington life.

When Americans see "special envoys" Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner negotiate with wealthy Arab states while padding their bank accounts from those same states, they understand what's going on.

There's nothing more anti-populist than such elite self-dealing.

On economic policy, the administration dramatically expanded its tariffs, including its "universal tariff" policy. Strategic, focused tariffs can work. But this was something else entirely.

Fact is, Joe and Jane in flyover country didn't vote for a trade war with Canada.

Even more to the point: Why did Trump's economists assume tariffing everything that moves is "populist" in the first place?

Reshoring supply chains is important. But the tradeoff between production and lowering prices is real. Higher tariffs and more supply-chain reshoring means higher prices.

Maybe that tradeoff is worth it. Maybe it isn't. But the American people have spoken, and they want lower prices over anything else. So populism means winding the tariffs down.

The story on the Iran war is similar.

Many isolationists complain that Trump reneged on his promise not to start any new Middle East wars. That's not quite fair. Trump already proved himself an Iran hawk when he withdrew from Barack Obama's calamitous nuclear deal, and the U.S. and Iran have technically been at war since 1979.

But the administration never actually made the case for the war to the American people. At times, Secretary of War Pete Hegseth alluded to war aims. But the people never heard the case from the commander in chief himself.

Populism means governing of, by and for the people. How could a purportedly populist president not even bother to try to sell the war to the public?

It was astonishing political malpractice.

Finally, a true populist movement needs to focus on real-world concerns, not the conspiratorial rabbit holes of social media.

The obsession with the "Epstein files" was always bogus and lame. And when White House Chief of Staff Susie Wiles reportedly told the terminally online Vice President JD Vance to take a break from the internet, she was onto something.

Real populism means boosting wages and lowering inflation — not staying up to the wee hours of the night trying to crack the Charlie Kirk murder case (news flash: it was Tyler Robinson) or blaming the Jews for stabbing the GOP in the back.

The good news is that most of the necessary changes are easy.

End the corruption. Wind down the global tariffs. Save face in Iran. Stop indulging brain-rotted conspiracists. Stop with the asinine lake name-change gimmicks. And get working quickly to lower gas and food prices.

Above all, make life easier, not harder, for ordinary Americans.

If this happens, the GOP will have a chance in 2028.

The MAGA movement died on Tuesday. But Trump's final two White House years should still reflect the original MAGA spirit: governance for the people.

news.title: Israel faces new era of sinking US support after election
news.text: JERUSALEM: Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's brash campaign posters are still up on Israeli public buses -- images of him, US President Donald Trump and soaring warjets that laud the two leaders attacking Iran together.Neither is now advertising the state of the two countries' alliance.A week after an inconclusive election for Netanyahu, Americans overwhelmingly rejected Trump and chose a Congress led by Democrats who want a tougher approach to Israel, whether on Iran, Gaza or settler violence in the occupied West Bank.The back-to-back elections look to many observers like a turning point, with Israel no longer able to take for granted the cover of the world's most powerful country."This is a new era. The confluence of the Gaza war and the war with Iran have really changed how mainstream Americans -- not people particularly concerned with the Israeli-Palestinian conflict -- see Israel," said Yael Sternhell, an expert on the United States at Tel Aviv University.Vice President JD Vance, assessing why his Republicans fared poorly, listed four ways to bring voters back, including ending the Iran war and changing "our relationship with Israel".Trump did not disagree. Just as voting was underway Tuesday, Trump said he had agreed with Netanyahu to end the $3.8 billion in annual US military aid to Israel by the end of this year, explicitly tying the decision to the US political mood..Not clear who can form a government, says Herzog following consultations.Netanyahu, Israel's longest-serving prime minister who has served on and off for nearly two decades, had eagerly sought Trump's endorsement but also acknowledged his country's growing isolation.In the final days of the campaign, he suggested Israel turn to cryptocurrencies to circumvent international sanctions he expected would intensify.Netanyahu has not commented on the US election or Trump's aid remarks.Amit Segal, a journalist known for his proximity to Netanyahu, posted that the political situation in the United States marked a "catastrophe" for Israel.- Can Eisenkot restore the alliance? -Opposition contender Gadi Eisenkot, who is trying to cobble together a coalition to oust Netanyahu, has cast himself as capable of repairing relations.In an English-language statement, the former military chief said he believed in "liberal values" and also wanted to work "closely and constructively" with Trump.Yair Golan, the main left-wing leader inside Eisenkot's bloc, called for Israel to restore a bipartisan approach destroyed by Netanyahu who he said promoted a "destructive Israeli narrative of eternal war and authoritarian rule"..Eisenkot tipped to seek Israel government with backing of Arab lists.Netanyahu boasted in his campaign about standing up to Democratic presidents including Barack Obama, who remains a hero for many Democrats. Netanyahu openly aligned with Republicans a decade ago to attack Obama's diplomacy on Iran."Netanyahu certainly rubs Democrats the wrong way and has made every effort to alienate them," Sternhell said."But Eisenkot can't just be a nicer man to receive a softer approach from this new Congress," she added. "He's going to need new policies."She said Eisenkot would likely enjoy Israeli public support for cracking down on extremist settlers, who have attacked Palestinians in the West Bank with virtual impunity.But Israel has shifted to the right, with wide initial support for the Gaza war.- Broadening criticism of Israel -The new Congress will include progressive Democrats such as Abdul El-Sayed, the first Muslim elected to the Senate, who describe the devastation in Gaza as genocide, an assertion rejected by Israel.Netanyahu "made a bet not only on the Republicans but almost personally on Trump", said Eli Kowaz, senior policy director of the Economic Cooperation Foundation, an Israeli think tank that backs a two-state solution with the Palestinians."These results show that bet had an expiry date," Kowaz said. "Also, for the first time, really, I think there's a realisation that it isn't only about the Democrats. It's a problem with the relationship with America.".Without US assistance, Israel still has its own major arms industry and retains a clear edge fighting non-state actors such as Hamas and Hezbollah, said Ehud Eilam, a former researcher for the Israeli defence ministry.But he said Israel would need to rely more on cheaper artillery or non-sophisticated bombs, further increasing risks of civilian casualties that have enraged international opinion."Israel can adjust to a new strategic reality of losing much and even all US military aid, but it will be tough for Israel. It will require Israel to consider hard choices such as taking huge loans or raising taxes," Eilam said.Kowaz said that Eisenkot, aware of politics in Washington, was trying to show he is interested in regional stability and strategic agreements and not just "an indefinite state of war"."He is definitely laying out a different vision for Israel's relationship with the United States.".Follow The New Indian Express channel on WhatsApp Download the TNIE app to stay with us and follow the latest

news.title: Top US diplomat says Venezuelan elections should 'ideally' be held next year
news.text:
NEW YORK, November 6. /TASS/. Elections in Venezuela would "ideally" be held next year, US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said.

However, he declined to guarantee the vote would take place before the end of US President Donald Trump’s term in office. According to Rubio, Venezuela still must take several critical steps to create the right conditions for elections.

Trump’s presidential term will expire on January 20, 2029. The US secretary of energy said in May that elections in Venezuela would be held while Trump was still in office in the US. Trump himself told Time magazine in early October that it was too early to hold elections in Venezuela.

Venezuela’s authorized president Delcy Rodriguez said in an address to the UN General Assembly that the country would hold a presidential election once its people considered the time right, not when they received orders from abroad.
news.summary: Marco Rubio declined to guarantee the vote would take place before the end of US President Donald Trump’s term in office

news.title: Trump warns Iran as Democrats plan war votes
news.text:
Washington: US President Donald Trump raised the prospect of further military action against Iran on Thursday (local time), even as senior House Democrats outlined plans to force votes to end the war and demand answers about its objectives and costs.

“I would rather not destroy the rest of the country, if possible, but maybe I’ll have to. You’ll know soon enough,” Trump told reporters at the White House.

He gave no timetable or targets for further action and did not announce that new strikes had been ordered.

The warning came as Democrats prepared their foreign-policy agenda for the next Congress, with Representative Gregory Meeks promising resolutions to terminate the conflict and Democratic Whip Katherine Clark questioning its goals and exit strategy.

Their statements preceded Trump’s latest remarks. They set out the congressional opposition confronting his Iran policy, rather than responses to Thursday afternoon’s warning.

Speaking during an Oval Office event, Trump defended the military campaign and said a decision would be made on whether to go further. He also reiterated his position that Iran must not acquire a nuclear weapon.

Asked about reports of proposals concerning Tehran’s nuclear programme, he said: “They’re not doing anything without our approval.”

Trump did not confirm the substance of any proposal or describe an agreed negotiating framework. His remarks left both the scope of potential military action and the diplomatic route unspecified.

Meeks, the senior Democrat on the House Foreign Affairs Committee, set out his plans in a November 4 letter seeking colleagues’ support to become its chairman.

“On the legislative front, I intend to bring resolutions to the floor to immediately terminate the President’s war with Iran and will prioritize clawing back Congress’s proper role in the making of American foreign policy,” he wrote.

The letter also proposed demanding public testimony from senior administration officials about the Iran war, Venezuela and disputes over congressional authority on military action and trade.

Meeks was describing an intended legislative and oversight agenda. The letter did not establish a date for a vote or identify a newly introduced resolution implementing that pledge.

Earlier, Clark told CNN that Democrats would press the administration about continued funding for the conflict and how it intended to bring American troops home safely.

Her office circulated excerpts of the interview before Trump’s afternoon remarks.

Clark accused the president of taking the country into “a reckless war that had no exit strategy, had no clear goals”, and blamed the conflict for increasing pressure on household fuel costs.

She said Democrats would seek discussions about the administration’s objectives and how to end the war while protecting Americans and US troops.

The two Democrats emphasised different avenues for challenging the administration: Meeks proposed floor resolutions and testimony, while Clark focused on funding, public costs and an exit strategy. Neither statement amounted to a new restriction already imposed on the president.

The Gulf conflict also concerns major Asian energy importers, including India. The International Energy Agency identifies the Strait of Hormuz as a critical oil transit route and lists India, China and Japan among the principal destinations for oil leaving the waterway.

news.title: Trump's 250-ft memorial arch in Washington on road to breaking ground after key federal panel votes to launch construction... but one hurdle could ruin it all
news.text:
A federal planning agency has greenlit Donald Trump's towering 250-foot 'Triumphal Arch' near downtown Washington, with construction potentially set to begin within 24 hours.

The National Capital Planning Commission (NCPC), a federal agency responsible for overseeing major construction and development in Washington, voted 8-4 in favor of the president's proposed arch, which is slated to be built near Arlington National Cemetery.

The decision clears a major hurdle for a project Trump has pursued as part of his efforts to reshape the capital region. The towering monument is set to stand 250 feet tall, roughly the height of a 25-story building.

Construction has now received official approval, with administration officials indicating that work could begin within 24 hours.

But the green light does not mean the project is entirely in the clear. The arch is still facing legal challenges, and a federal judge is expected to rule soon on whether construction should be blocked.

The commission's final vote came after nine and a half hours of deliberations and testimony from scores of people opposed to the project.

The cost also remains uncertain. While some estimates have put the price tag as high as $100 million, it is unclear exactly how much the monument will cost or how it will be funded.

This is a breaking news story...
news.summary: The decision clears a major hurdle for a project Trump has pursued as part of his efforts to reshape the capital region. The  massive monument is set to stand 250 feet tall.

news.title: Pete Hegseth First, Todd Blanche Next? Democrats Eye Impeachment Push
news.text: Democrats are preparing to ramp up congressional scrutiny of the Trump administration after sweeping both chambers in the midterm elections, with Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth already facing an impeachment push and Attorney General Todd Blanche emerging as another potential target. Hegseth could face an impeachment vote as soon as next week, with Republican Representative Thomas Massie planning to force a House vote on articles of impeachment when lawmakers return to Washington. Massie reiterated his plans Thursday, suggesting President Donald Trump should replace Hegseth “while he can still get the replacements confirmed in the Senate.” “Also, my Hegseth impeachment resolution is a much gentler version of what's coming when Dem's control Congress. They'll have hearings & trials,” Massie wrote on X. Hegseth has pushed back against the impeachment effort, calling the articles a "sham" and comparing them to the two impeachment proceedings against Trump. "Didn't work against President Trump, and it won't work with me. You can rest assured of that," Hegseth said in a lengthy video posted to X Thursday. He also accused Democrats and what he called "deep state radicals" of pursuing "the politics of personal destruction." Trump defended Hegseth on Thursday, telling reporters the defense secretary had done a “fantastic job” when asked about possible staffing changes. The president also said he believed it would take Iran 25 years to rebuild from the war. Blanche Could Also Face Impeachment Calls Representative Jamie Raskin, the Maryland Democrat expected to chair the House Judiciary Committee, said Thursday that Blanche could also face impeachment hearings. Raskin accused the Justice Department under Blanche of pursuing Trump's political opponents while failing to adequately address other matters, including the Jeffrey Epstein files. "Look at all of the fraudulent prosecutions that they've engaged in against people like James Comey, like Letitia James, like Adam Schiff, like Mark Kelly, like Maggie Goodlander and Jason Crow, and on and on," Raskin told MS NOW on Thursday. "The Department of Justice has clearly become a Department of Injustice — an instrument of revenge, political revenge for the president," he said. At least two other House Democrats have raised the prospect of impeaching Blanche. Representative Hank Johnson, a Georgia Democrat, said he believes the attorney general's conduct warrants impeachment and removal from office. "I personally believe that the offenses of Todd Blanche demand that he be impeached and convicted and removed from office," Johnson said on SiriusXM's The Dan Abrams Show. "I think his efforts to undermine the rule of law can't go unaddressed." Representative Deborah Ross, a North Carolina Democrat, also voiced support for impeachment, while saying lawmakers should begin with Hegseth. Asked whether she supported impeaching Blanche, Ross said "100%" before adding: "I think we should start with Hegseth." No formal impeachment resolution against Blanche has been announced. Newsweek has reached out to the Justice Department and the Pentagon for further comment. Democrats Back Calls for Hegseth's Removal Massie, a Kentucky Republican and frequent Trump critic, introduced eight articles of impeachment against Hegseth on September 15. They accuse the defense secretary of violating the Constitution and federal law, including by conducting military operations in Iran without congressional authorization and continuing hostilities in violation of the War Powers Resolution. Pentagon spokesman Sean Parnell said Hegseth was "100% committed to leading the Department until the end of President Trump's term in office" and would not be deterred by what he described as partisan investigations. Massie's effort has drawn support from Democrats who have separately called for Hegseth to leave the Pentagon. "Secretary Hegseth has been nothing short of a disaster for the Pentagon and for America's standing in the world," Representative Salud Carbajal, a California Democrat who sits on the House Armed Services Committee, told The Hill on Wednesday. Representative Eugene Vindman, a Virginia Democrat and former Army colonel who also serves on the Armed Services Committee, has likewise said Hegseth's conduct warrants impeachment. "His recklessness, staggering lack of judgment, and repeated failures have put American service members at risk and undermined our national security," Vindman told The Hill. House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries has also criticized Hegseth. On Thursday, he posted on X: "Why is Pete Hegseth still around?" Craig Agranoff, political professor at Florida Atlantic University, told Newsweek earlier Thursday that public White House support makes an “immediate dismissal less likely than a drawn-out fight." Newsweek’s reporters and editors used Martyn, our AI assistant, to produce this story. Learn more about Martyn here. Contact Newsweek editors on this story: Steven Frank and Edward T. Cummins
news.summary: Democrats are signaling tougher oversight of Trump officials, with some lawmakers raising the prospect of impeachment.

news.title: Ukraine-Russia war live: Trump claims ‘big, beautiful’ deal in the works as UK refuses to invite Putin to G20
news.text:
US president Donald Trump has claimed that Russia's war on Ukraine was close to being settled and that ending it might involve all of Europe.

Trump said he met privately with Russian special envoy Kirill Dmitriev at the White House as first lady, Melania Trump, ​hosted ​representatives from Kyiv and Moscow.

news.title: 'JD, habibi.' Arabs celebrate El-Sayed's use of a term of affection in his victory speech

news.title: Trump's DC arch gets key approval, but judge could still block it
news.text:
WASHINGTON - President Donald Trump's proposed 250-foot triumphal arch in Washington, DC, won a key approval on Nov. 5, which could lead to construction beginning quickly on the latest major project in his drive to reshape the U.S. capital.

The National Capital Planning Commission voted to approve the project after hearing from about 100 opponents, including Democratic lawmakers.

"It will snarl traffic for years, impact the nearby airport, and present even more serious threats to public safety that this commission has refused to acknowledge and grapple with," said Rep. Don Beyer, who represents northern Virginia.

A judge considering several legal challenges could still block the start of construction. But if it gets the go-ahead, the Justice Department has said it expects an initial six to eight months of construction focused on excavation and foundation work to begin this week.

Above-ground construction would start in May 2027 at the earliest, with the job expected to take 33 to 39 months total.

The National Park Service may also issue a permit or other authorization on Nov. 5, and launch construction this week, the government said in a court filing.

The arch is among several costly projects Trump is pushing in Washington despite opposition from local officials and preservationists. They include rebuilding the Reflecting Pool at the Lincoln Memorial, constructing a massive White House ballroom and overhauling the Kennedy Center for the Performing Arts.

The arch has faced significant opposition in the courts. The state of Virginia and the District of Columbia sued the National Park Service and the Department of the Interior on Oct. 31, seeking to halt the start of construction, calling it "legally indefensible" and arguing that Congress has not approved it.

The government contends Congress approved the arch more than 100 years ago when it also authorized construction of a bridge across the Potomac River.

At an event on Nov. 2 to highlight improvements to the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool, Trump said the arch would also serve as a military asset and would be able to house drones and snipers.

"It's right smack in the middle of everything, so very important for our military. But from a beautification standpoint, it'll be the most beautiful arch in the world," Trump said.

The arch, which would include an eternal flame and floodlights to make it visible to pilots, would be situated across the Potomac River from the Lincoln Memorial on a highway roundabout near the entrance to Arlington National Cemetery.

It would resemble the Arc de Triomphe in Paris, but stand more than 80 feet taller. It would also be nearly as tall as the U.S. Capitol, which, at 288 feet, can be seen across much of Washington. The site is near airplanes' final approach to Ronald Reagan Washington National Airport.

A rendering showed the flame would be held by a 60-foot-tall gold, winged female figure positioned atop the arch and flanked by gold flying eagles.

(Reporting by David Shepardson; Editing by Chris Sanders and Edmund Klamann)

news.title: US stocks lose $2.5 trillion as AI investment fears trigger Wall Street sell-off
news.text: New York Concerns over a possible slowdown in artificial intelligence-related investments wiped out around USD 2.5 trillion in US stock market value on Thursday, as a sharp sell-off in technology stocks erased Wall Street’s post-election rally, CNN reported. The sell-off came amid fears that gains by the Democratic Party in the US midterm elections could lead to restrictions on data centre expansion and slow down the country’s artificial intelligence infrastructure development. Nasdaq suffers worst single-day fall since April 2025 The technology-heavy Nasdaq Composite suffered its worst single-day fall since April 2025, when US President Donald Trump announced sweeping global tariffs. The decline also dragged down broader market indices, with the S&P 500 and Dow Jones Industrial Average recording their worst trading sessions since April 2025. The Nasdaq plunged 5.52 per cent to close at 24,315.00, falling more than 10 per cent below the record level it had reached last month and entering correction territory. The S&P 500 declined 4.36 per cent to settle at 7,353.73, while the Dow Jones Industrial Average dropped 1,833.06 points, or 3.44 per cent, to close at 51,523.06. The sharp losses erased the gains made during Wednesday’s post-election rally, when the Dow had surged more than 1,500 points, marking its best trading day since April 2025. The S&P 500 and Nasdaq had also gained more than 1 per cent each during that session. Data centre restrictions fuel technology stock sell-off Investors turned cautious about technology companies after concerns emerged that Democratic gains in both chambers of Congress and key gubernatorial races could affect the expansion of data centres in the United States. On Wednesday, shares of major technology companies, including Amazon, Meta and Google, had rallied on expectations that new restrictions could reduce their spending on data centres and free up cash, potentially improving profitability. However, investors reversed those trades on Thursday amid concerns that the proposed restrictions could ultimately hurt the technology sector, CNN reported. Semiconductor stocks bear the brunt of selling Semiconductor companies and businesses linked to data centre infrastructure witnessed heavy selling. Broadcom shares fell 10 per cent, while Nvidia declined 9 per cent. Oracle also dropped almost 7 per cent. Keith Lerner, Chief Investment Officer at Truist Advisory Services, described the volatile market movements this week as more of a knee-jerk reaction than a clear indication of how technology stocks could perform under Democratic control of Congress, according to CNN. The sharp decline reflects growing investor concerns over the future pace of artificial intelligence infrastructure investments in the United States, particularly as data centre expansion and related technology spending remain under market focus.
news.summary: Investors reversed earlier technology stock gains as concerns over potential policy changes raised questions about future artificial intelligence infrastructure spending

news.title: Melania hosts Russia and Ukraine as Trump touts deal for ‘all of Europe’
news.text:
Washington: US President Donald Trump predicted Thursday an imminent deal with Russia covering Ukraine and “all of Europe,” after his wife, First Lady Melania Trump, hosted officials from the two warring countries at the White House.

Trump revealed that he had an unscheduled meeting with Kirill Dmitriev, Russian President Vladimir Putin’s envoy, following his involvement in the event hosted by the US first lady.

Trump’s comments will fuel Ukrainian and European fears that he is pivoting toward the Kremlin for a larger deal that could reduce the US military presence on the continent and give Moscow more sway.

They also come the week before three-way talks between Russia, Ukraine and the United States are due to resume in Abu Dhabi for the first time since February.

While Melania called for an “enduring” Ukraine ceasefire to follow up the brief truce she brokered in a Russian-occupied town, her 80-year-old husband indicated that an unspecified “very big” deal was close.

“I can’t tell you what I discussed. But I’m just telling you, it’s going to be an agreement, it’s going to be a big agreement,” Trump told reporters in the Oval Office when asked about his talks with Dmitriev.

“It’s going to be very big. It’s going to involve more than Ukraine, and I could even say it might involve all of Europe. It’s going to be a big, beautiful agreement, and everyone’s going to be thrilled.”

Trump said he had not met with Ukrainian officials who were also at the White House on Thursday.

- ‘More enduring’ -

The US president’s efforts to end the war he promised to stop within 24 hours of taking office have ebbed and flowed, but his wife’s quiet diplomatic efforts have stepped up.

The unprecedented meeting at the White House between Russian and Ukrainian officials hoped to build on a localized six-day truce in the starvation-hit Ukrainian city of Oleshky.

“Now we must use the courage we brought to Oleshky to find common ground through a shared concern for the suffering of innocent people,” the first lady told reporters.

“Together, we can create something more enduring than a temporary ceasefire.”

The Slovenian-born former model, 56, said she was sending the envoys back with personal letters to Putin and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky.

The Ukrainian president awarded Melania Trump a national honor for her role in brokering the Oleshky ceasefire, which a Ukrainian official personally presented to her at the White House.

Dmitriev said he thanked the US first lady on Putin’s behalf for her “distinguished humanitarian role.”

The White House meeting also reunited Russia’s human rights ombudsman Yana Lantratova — who has been sanctioned by Britain — and her counterpart from Kyiv, Dmytro Lubinets, who formed an unlikely bond during the Oleshky ceasefire.

‘Security architecture’ 

The US first lady stunned the world when she announced in October 2025 that she had established a secret channel of communication with Putin in a bid to reunite war-separated children.

She has since played a growing but still behind-the-scenes diplomatic role in the Ukraine conflict — even as her husband campaigns openly to win the Nobel Peace Prize despite his own failed efforts to end the war.

In Kyiv, Zelensky said he had a “very detailed, hour-and-a-half-long” conversation with US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner ahead of the Abu Dhabi talks.

The talks have revived hopes for ending the grinding war, although a recent rapprochement between Donald Trump and Putin has raised concerns the United States could turn its back on Kyiv.

Kushner said he met Ukrainian, NATO and European officials in Brussels to discuss “security guarantees for Ukraine and a broader European security architecture.”

Washington has also reportedly been discussing possible business deals with Russia as part of a general Ukraine deal.
news.summary: US President Donald Trump expressed optimism about a forthcoming deal with Russia involving Ukraine and Europe following a White House event hosted by First Lady Melania Trump with officials from the two countries.

news.title: Trump teases ‘big agreement’ after meeting Putin envoy but not with Ukrainian officials
news.text:
President Donald Trump confirmed holding talks with Vladimir Putin’s envoy at the White House on Thursday, but did not meet visiting Ukrainian officials.

Speaking to reporters in the Oval Office, Trump acknowledged his conversation with Kirill Dmitriev. "I can’t tell you what I discussed," Trump said.

Asked if he had met Ukrainian representatives, Trump said he had not. 

Officials from both countries were at the White House for an occasion honouring Melania Trump’s work brokering a ceasefire in Oleshky.

Having declined to provide details regarding his discussion with Dmitriev, Trump indicated that a wider arrangement was taking shape.

"Its going to be an agreement, it’s going to be a big agreement and it’s going to involve more than Ukraine," Trump said, noting that it could potentially encompass the whole of Europe.

Russian President Vladimir Putin’s envoy joined Melania Trump at the White House on Thursday as she brought together Russian and Ukrainian officials to recognise the localized ceasefire she negotiated between the two nations in a besieged Ukrainian village.

Addressing the gathering at her invitation, Dmitriev offered his gratitude to the first lady for her "distinguished humanitarian role" in securing the six-day truce.

Dmitriev noted that Putin personally issued directions regarding the operation and passed on his appreciation to Melania Trump. Representatives from Ukraine also took part in the event marking the ceasefire, which was signed Oct. 23.

The head of the parliamentary faction of President Volodymyr Zelenskyy’s party, Davyd Arakhamia, and Ukraine’s human rights ombudsman, Dmytro Lubinets, also spoke at the event.

Arakhamia told the first lady she did an “amazing job" and encouraged her to keep helping the Ukrainian people, who have endured more than four years of war after Putin sent his troops across the border and invaded the country in 2022.

“Definitely we would like to ask you to keep going and to find new missions and to de-escalate more as much as possible,” Arakhamia said.

The first lady has worked with both countries since last year to reunite families separated by the war. So far, she has helped nearly three dozen children return to their relatives.

She said Thursday that she hoped the Oleshky ceasefire could become more enduring and more widespread.

“Let Oleshky be the modest spark that grows into a lasting flame of peace,” she said.

Peace between Russia and Ukraine so far has eluded President Trump, who alternately has pressed Russia and Ukraine to end the war since he returned to office nearly two years ago.

Zelenskyy, in a speech in Spain on Friday, said the operation in Oleshky proved “something very simple. When Putin wants the fighting to stop, it stops. And there was real silence, no attacks some days, and we saved hundreds of lives.”

The ceasefire is the latest example of how Melania Trump has become more involved in foreign affairs than some of her recent predecessors, who typically travel abroad to spread U.S. goodwill and avoid involvement with warring countries.

In 2022, months after Russia invaded Ukraine, first lady Jill Biden traveled to western Ukraine to visit with Zelenskyy's wife in a town far away from the front lines. Under tight security, first lady Laura Bush made several visits to war-torn Afghanistan.

In an announcement that came as a surprise, the White House said on Oct. 23 that the first lady had brokered the ceasefire to help with the delivery of much-needed humanitarian aid and to allow civilians to evacuate from a place she described as being “on the brink of disaster.”

Ukrainian, Russian and U.S. negotiators earlier that day had reached an agreement to deliver relief to Oleshky in the war-divided region of Kherson in southern Ukraine.

The local ceasefire was in effect from Oct. 27 to Nov. 1 and amounted to the most significant truce since Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine.

An estimated 2,000 people remained in Oleshky when the temporary truce took hold. They were offered the choice of evacuating to territory controlled by Ukraine or Russia, or remaining in the city with replenished food and medical supplies.

Supplies were delivered during the six-day window while hundreds of Oleshky residents crossed into Ukrainian-held territory in a major evacuation operation.

Melania Trump said Thursday that nearly 800 people had evacuated Oleshky, and she described how she initiated talks with officials in both countries after learning about the situation at an event she held on the sidelines of the U.N. General Assembly session in September. She said she and her top adviser, Marc Beckman, worked directly with Russian and Ukrainian leadership to define the terms of the ceasefire.

Food and medical supplies had been scarce for months in Oleshky, once a city of about 24,000 residents that sits on the Dnipro River separating Ukrainian forces from the city’s Russian occupiers. There is no electricity, heat or running water.

Oleshky was captured by Moscow’s forces on the first day of Russia’s full-scale invasion. Its buildings were shelled and burned, and its infrastructure damaged. In June 2023, floodwaters inundated the city after the Kakhovka Dam collapsed from an explosion that an investigation found was likely caused by the Russian military. Hundreds of residents were killed.

Those left in the city along Ukraine’s southeastern front face death from hunger or disease as another harsh winter looms. Ukraine has appealed repeatedly for a local ceasefire to organize evacuations. Russia, as the occupying power, is obligated by international law to ensure civilians under its control have what they need to survive.

The first lady presented Putin and Zelenskyy's representatives with large white envelopes and asked them to deliver her personal letter to each leader. Dmitriev presented her with a painting from an 11-year-old girl while Zelenskyy sent her a Ukrainian award recognizing her role in the ceasefire.
news.summary: Representatives from both countries were at the White House for an event honoring Melania Trump’s work brokering a ceasefire in Oleshky
news.author: Darlene Superville

news.title: US seeks to address security concerns of all sides in talks — Trump’s son-in-law
news.text:
WASHINGTON, November 6. /TASS/. The Washington administration seeks to address the security interests of all sides in consultations on resolving the Ukraine conflict, US President Donald Trump’s son-in-law Jared Kushner said.

"Our objective is to address the security concerns of all sides through practical, mutually agreed arrangements that reduce the risk of future conflict," he wrote on X.

"Next week in Abu Dhabi, the United States will convene the first trilateral peace discussions with Ukraine and Russia since February. We have been working with both parties to develop serious proposals that can make the discussions as substantive and productive as possible," Kushner added.

news.title: Not clear who can form a government, says Herzog following consultations
news.text: JERUSALEM: After two days of consultations with leaders of parties elected to the Knesset (Israeli parliament), President Isaac Herzog on Thursday evening said it is not clear to him who has the ability to form a government."I would like to update the public following the conclusion of the round of consultations with the Knesset factions. I met with the representatives of all the factions. The discussions were open, candid, and also probing. I asked difficult questions in an effort to help the parties and the public to break free from set ways of thinking and open their minds to other paths", Herzog said."The picture is as follows: the representatives of factions totalling 67 members of Knesset recommended the Leader of the Yashar! party, Gadi Eisenkot, to form a government, while the representatives of factions totalling 46 members of Knesset recommended the Prime Minister and Leader of the Likud party, Benjamin Netanyahu, to form a government", he added.However, he went on to say that "the results of the consultations may appear clear, but the authority vested in me by law is to determine who has the ability to form a government, and that is not entirely clear, given the mutual vetoes between the blocs and within the blocs themselves." The Israeli President said that he would task a member of the Knesset with forming a government on Sunday.The statement is surprising because, by precedent, the elected member with the most recommendations is generally tasked by the President to form a government."I will try to determine this directly and quickly, in personal talks with some of the party leaders. In these talks, I intend to leave no stone unturned in an effort to reach out and build a stable and good government for the people of Israel," Herzog stressed. .The bloc led by Netanyahu won 53 seats in the 120-member house in the October 27 polls.The anti-Netanyahu bloc, also being described as the 'change bloc' got 48 with the remaining 19 going to the Arab parties in a fractured mandate.United Torah Judaism, a party in the Netanyahu bloc, decided not to recommend him, bringing the number of recommendations for the incumbent Prime Minister to 46.The Arab parties, on the other hand, grudgingly recommended Eisenkot, declaring their intent to oust Netanyahu.However, both blocs have shown a general aversion towards aligning with the Arab parties and most of the parties in both blocs, except the Democrats, have shown an aversion to sitting with the Arab parties in a government.The sticking point in bringing the Arab parties into a governing coalition revolves around their reluctance to declare Hamas a terrorist organisation, something unacceptable to the majority of the Jewish population following the deadly attacks of October 7, 2023.Earlier during the day, Ra'am party leader Mansour Abbas, after recommending Eisenkot, reiterated his support for a two-state solution and US President Donald Trump's Gaza plan, including calling for "Hamas and all the military or armed organisations to be disarmed," but fell short of calling Hamas a terrorist organisation..Follow The New Indian Express channel on WhatsApp Download the TNIE app to stay with us and follow the latest

news.title: Jamie Dimon vowed to fight Clarity Act stablecoin yields; Democratic win may kill bill
news.text: The cryptocurrency industry's efforts to secure a comprehensive US regulatory framework could face a major setback after Democrats won control of both chambers of Congress in the midterm elections, with analysts warning that the long-debated CLARITY Act may struggle to advance. The development comes months after JPMorgan Chase CEO Jamie Dimon vowed to fight provisions that could allow yield-paying stablecoins, arguing that such products pose risks similar to those seen in shadow banking. According to a CoinDesk report, several industry observers believe the Democratic victory has significantly reduced the chances of the CLARITY Act passing in its current form. Mati Greenspan, founder of Quantum Economics, described the Democratic sweep as potentially "the final nail in the CLARITY Act's coffin," noting that the legislation failed to clear a procedural Senate vote even when Republicans controlled both chambers. He said the crypto sector may now have to restart negotiations under a new political landscape.Jamie Dimon’s warning on CLARITY ActIn a Fox Business interview reported by The Globe and Mail in July, Dimon sharpened his criticism of the Digital Asset Market Clarity (CLARITY) Act, saying he feared yield-paying stablecoins could cause a “shadow banking” crisis. “We’ll fight it. If we lose, we lose, and we’ll live,” he said. Dimon argues that such tokens are effectively unregulated deposit-like products. Without capital requirements, he says, they could destabilise markets in a way similar to shadow banking in the 2008 financial crisis. In May, Dimon criticised Coinbase CEO Brian Armstrong in a Fox Business interview, according to Bloomberg, using crude language to dismiss him. He said banks “will not accept” the current version of the bill.The bank-crypto fightThe CLARITY Act, intended to set a federal framework for digital assets, passed the House last year. It stalled in the Senate over whether crypto firms can pay yield on stablecoins. A compromise reached in May would ban passive rewards earned simply by holding tokens, but allow activity-based rewards tied to transactions or platform use.Coinbase and other exchanges back yield-bearing stablecoins, arguing they expand consumer choice and innovation. Banks, led by Dimon and the American Bankers Association, want them banned outright to protect deposits and financial stability. A ban would hit Circle, issuer of the USDC stablecoin, which earns interest on the cash and Treasuries backing its tokens, and Coinbase, which shares in Circle’s reserve income and earns fees from stablecoin trading.Democratic sweepCoinDesk reported that the crypto industry’s hopes for a regulatory framework took another blow when Democrats won both chambers. “For crypto, the Democratic sweep may well be the final nail in the Clarity Act’s coffin,” said Mati Greenspan, founder of Quantum Economics. He noted the bill couldn’t even clear a procedural vote in September, when Republicans controlled both chambers, and that the industry may now have to start from scratch in a divided Washington.Stefan Muehlbauer, head of US government affairs at CertiK, said the bill is likely dead in its current form. Anton Golub said crypto political action groups spent about $170.5 million on the elections, with at least $125.5 million going to Republicans. Despite Republican control of Congress and a crypto-friendly President Donald Trump, the bill failed to advance in September. Golub said Trump made regulators friendlier to the industry, but his family’s crypto involvement also gave Democrats a reason to oppose crypto-friendly legislation.Greater scrutiny expected for crypto sectorSeveral industry participants expect Democrats to take a more aggressive approach toward crypto oversight. CoinDesk reported that lawmakers could focus on issues including anti-money laundering controls, cybersecurity practices and consumer protection measures.Muehlbauer said congressional hearings and investigations may examine both cryptocurrency companies and President Trump's crypto-related business interests. Meanwhile, Shady El Damaty, co-founder of Human.tech, predicted increased scrutiny of tokenised stock offerings and broader crypto expansion efforts by trading platforms.Not everyone believes the legislation is beyond saving. Brent Fulfer, co-founder of venture capital firm TBV, noted that more than 70 House Democrats previously supported the CLARITY Act and argued that a revised bill with stronger safeguards and bipartisan backing could still gain traction.Crypto products expected to keep expandingWhile the regulatory outlook has become more uncertain, some industry executives believe innovation in digital asset products will continue. Golub said products such as perpetual futures are likely to grow beyond cryptocurrencies and expand into equities and other traditional financial markets.Jason Fernandes, founder of AdLunam, said the crypto industry should engage constructively with Democratic lawmakers rather than oppose stricter oversight outright. According to Fernandes, carefully targeted regulation and enforcement against bad actors could ultimately strengthen the broader crypto ecosystem.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.
news.summary: The recent midterm elections have ushered in Democratic dominance over both Congressional chambers, posing challenges for the CLARITY Act's advancement. Analysts predict a tough road ahead due to shifting political dynamics. Jamie Dimon has raised alarms about yield-paying stablecoins, deeming them high-risk financial assets. As Congress ramps up regulatory focus on cryptocurrency, some experts hold onto hope for a reimagined CLARITY Act that could still attract bipartisan backing.

news.title: Are the Republicans abandoning Trump? It’s ’knives out’ after the midterm loss
news.text:
The US midterms have delivered a bruising defeat to Donald Trump and the Republican Party. Democrats are projected to win more than 250 House seats, heading toward their largest majority since 2008, and have even taken control of the US Senate.
The fallout from the November 3 results has left the Republicans reeling and trying to come up with reasons for their dismal performance. It has left the GOP struggling with a power battle within its ranks, as leaders begin to position themselves for 2028 when the presidential elections are due.
Reports have already emerged of firings, US Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth is on the chopping block, and possible resignations, with the US Secretary of State possibly looking to exit the Trump Cabinet.
Let the infighting begin
In the immediate aftermath of the US midterm results, in which the Republicans suffered a broad rebuke, top leaders from the GOP began to pin blame on the Iran war for their loss.
US Vice President JD Vance, in a rather lengthy post on X, blamed the conflict that began in February for the party’s poor showing at the polls. “The reason we lost is the war,” he wrote, adding that the voters were angry with the administration over the Iran war, cost of living and inflation, and the current US relationship with Israel, which receives billions of dollars in annual US aid.
 US Vice President JD Vance has blamed the loss at the US midterms on the Iran war. File image/Reuters
“But everyone knows why we lost. And any honest conversation about where we go from here must start there.”
He further urged Republicans to take their anger and “get back to the work of saving our country”.
Shortly after his message, reports emerged that the American vice president has begun work on forging a new political alliance targeting disaffected supporters of President Donald Trump.
Paul Musgrave, associate professor of government at Georgetown University in Qatar, told Al Jazeera that Vance “is trying to represent a more isolationist wing of the Republican Party, and is willing to walk away from the war and probably other commitments to win favour with a large part of the Trump base”.
Meanwhile, Ted Cruz, the Senator from Texas, also blamed the conflict for the party’s loss, saying in an episode of his podcast on Wednesday that it “should have been brief, decisive, and over”. He also wrote on X that the war had “dragged on too long” and that Washington “should never, under any circumstances, give the Ayatollah billions of dollars”.
 Florida Governor Ron DeSantis declared the elections to be “close to an extinction-level event” for their party. File image/Reuters
Florida governor Ron DeSantis further declared this week’s elections to be “close to an extinction-level event” for their party. He said that Republicans had promised they would publish the Epstein files, which included a vast array of documents and correspondence tied to the disgraced financier. He said: “And then you actually have people in the Congress voting against release [of the Epstein files] when the attorney general said she had all this horrific stuff on her desk and that people were going to be held accountable.”
He further demanded that Congress outlaw stock trading by lawmakers — and extend the prohibition to the executive branch.
In what can be perceived as a positioning move, the outgoing governor touted Florida to be the only state out of the 10 largest that would be controlled by Republicans after the midterms. “We’ve built up a record of achievement,” DeSantis said. “We’ve earned trust from a number of our voters that, even in the worst situation that you can imagine politically, we were able to hold the line.”
Other senior leaders of the Republican party also began to vent their ire. Senator John Cornyn of Texas wrote in a Wall Street Journal op-ed that Republicans made a series of “unforced political errors,” including being told to embrace scandal-plagued nominee Ken Paxton, who defeated him in a primary race.
Trump staring at a possible Rubio exit
Amid this in-fighting within the Republicans, US President Trump also has to grapple with the likelihood of his US Secretary of State Marco Rubio resigning.
Following the midterm losses, reports emerged that Rubio is reportedly considering leaving President Donald Trump’s administration, possibly to launch a presidential campaign in 2028. “He hasn’t made a decision about whether to quit his posts as top US diplomat and national security adviser, and there is no timetable on a possible departure,” said sources in a Bloomberg report.
 US Secretary of State Marco Rubio is facing speculation that he could leave President Donald Trump’s administration to prepare for a 2028 presidential campaign after the drubbing the Republicans faced in the midterms. File image/Reuters
Rubio had gone up against Trump in the 2016 Republican primary but had lost then. After joining the Trump Cabinet, he has been rumoured to be considering another run for president, and his chances of winning the 2028 GOP nomination are second to Vice President JD Vance on the prediction market site Kalshi.
Another reported Rubio insider told The Independent that it made sense for the US Secretary of State to step down and leave the administration. “Rubio is the leading candidate at the moment to be the [Republican] nominee. He’s definitely ahead of Vance.
“But he cannot run while he is still secretary of state, and being tied to the administration will only harm his prospects anyway.”
However, Rubio has dismissed reports of him leaving his position, telling the New York Times, “It has always been my plan to work for President Donald Trump until the end of his term.”
On reports that he was considering an exit from the Trump administration, he further added: “I don’t know where these things come from, to be honest with you.”
Dylan Johnson, Assistant Secretary of State for global public affairs, also called the Bloomberg article “totally made up”. He also called the report by The Independent as “completely baseless fake news”.
Hegseth hangs on by a thread
And while Rubio is dismissing reports of his possible departure, US Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth is under growing pressure, with murmurs of him being fired becoming louder.
 US Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth is also under growing pressure, with many Republicans blaming him for the party's rout. File image/Reuters
Many within the GOP believe that Hegseth hard-sold the Iran war to Trump. Moreover, Hegseth has been accused of not being forthright about the damage to US bases in West Asia and the severity of troop casualties. He has also purged dozens of high-ranking military officers, while denying promotions to others on dubious grounds.
But US President Donald Trump has stood by Hegseth so far, insisting that “he’s doing a very good job” when asked whether he was going to replace the Pentagon chief.
As of now, nothing is certain in the Republican Party. But the latest developments are reflective of the new world Trump and his administration are facing.
With inputs from agencies

news.title: US' 2 Biggest Cities Now Have Indian-Origin Mayors
news.text: The results of US midterm elections have been disheartening for President Donald Trump and Republicans as they now have no control either in the Senate or House of Representatives. news.title: Petitions to Replace Chuck Schumer Pass 100,000 Signatures Day After Launch
news.text: Petitions calling for Senate Democrats to choose a new majority leader, opposed to current Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, have surpassed 100,000 signatures on Thursday. The petitions, both created on Wednesday, come on the heels of sweeping Democratic wins this midterm cycle that saw the House and Senate flip in their favor. President Donald Trump attempted to distance himself from the blue wave, saying he wasn't on the ballot, but if he were, "we would have won IN A LANDSLIDE!" One petition titled "Senate Democrats: CHOOSE A NEW MAJORITY LEADER" has 43,446 verified signatures and says, "We believe Democratic leadership should represent Democratic voters, not just the Democratic establishment," and that Schumer is not the right choice. A second petition titled "Replace Chuck Schumer as Senate Majority Leader" had 75,402 verified signatures as of 9:23 p.m. ET Thursday. The petition says Schumer "folds when it matters," pointing to previous legislation. The petition highlights the new Democratic senators elected into office, like Maine's Troy Jackson and Kansas' Adam Hamilton, saying that they have publicly announced they won't back Schumer as leader. The petition asks for every Democratic senator "to choose a leader who will fight for real progressive values." On Wednesday, Schumer was asked about the newly elected candidates who say they won't back him: "The issue is not me. I'll be reelected as majority leader. But the issue is focusing on the American people and what they want.” Newsweek reached out to Schumer's office on Thursday night for comment. What To Know Other newly elected Democratic senators like South Carolina's Annie Andrews and Michigan's Abdul El-Sayed have been asked if they'd support Schumer as majority leader. Andrews told Fox News' Bret Baier, "I believe it's time for a generational change on both sides of the aisle," when questioned about Schumer on Thursday. Minnesota Senator-elect Peggy Flanagan said on Wednesday in part, “I think it’s time for new leadership.” El-Sayed did not commit to backing Schumer and said that he would adamantly support Chris Van Hollen of Maryland, should he decide to pursue the position, while speaking with CNN's Kate Bolduan. The petition titled "Replace Chuck Schumer as Senate Majority Leader" was started by Laura Ciocia, the change.org website says. It has over 21,000 shares and 600 comments. It calls out Schumer for opposing former President Barack Obama's Iran nuclear deal over a decade ago, and for reportedly taking pro-Israel lobby money. The petition says progressives who want international law and human rights at the center of policy involving Gaza and Israel "cannot count on a leader funded this way." OpenSecrets, a political transparency group, shows that from 1990-2024, Schumer was a "pro-Israel" recipient of $1,727,974. The petition titled "Senate Democrats: CHOOSE A NEW MAJORITY LEADER" was started by Chris Sader, the website says, and has over 300 comments and nearly 9,000 shares. Petition to Replace Hakeem Jeffries Hits Over 750,000 A similar change.org petition was launched calling for House Democrats not to back Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries in a bid for House speaker. The petition, started by Nicole Whitted, had 762,343 verified signatures as of 9:10 p.m. ET Thursday, had been shared nearly 500,000 times and had over 15,000 comments. The petition says that "Nicole Whitted is a Change Ambassador who receives compensation in connection with this petition." The petition says Jeffries is not the right choice for House majority leader, adding, "We are calling on every member of the incoming 120th Congress to vote against Hakeem Jeffries for Speaker in January 2027 and choose a different candidate." Actor Mark Ruffalo, an outspoken supporter of progressive policies, posted the petition to his X account on Wednesday, adding, "Sign this petition if you want a new speaker of the house." Newsweek’s reporters and editors used Martyn, our AI assistant, to produce this story. Learn more about Martyn here. Contact Newsweek editors on this story: Edward T. Cummins
news.summary: The petitions, both created on Wednesday, come on the heels of sweeping Democratic wins this midterm cycle.

news.title: Kushner Unveils Five-Point European Security Plan Ahead of Ukraine-Russia Peace Talks
news.text:
US President Donald Trump’s son-in-law and senior negotiator Jared Kushner outlined five objectives for a broader European security framework on Thursday, Nov. 5, ahead of planned US-mediated peace talks between Ukraine and Russia in Abu Dhabi next week.

In a statement posted on X, Kushner said Trump had advanced discussions with several European leaders about establishing long-term security arrangements intended to prevent future conflicts.

The proposal follows negotiations in Brussels involving Ukraine, NATO, the European Union and other European partners.

“Our objective is to develop practical arrangements that address the security concerns of all sides, reduce the risk of future conflict, and create a more stable and predictable security environment,” Kushner wrote.

Five goals for European security

Kushner outlined five principal objectives:

 Permanent security consultations. Reliable crisis communications. Greater military transparency. Reciprocal measures to reduce escalation risks. A lasting framework for European security and stability. 

He said Europe and Russia had struggled for more than three decades to establish sustainable security arrangements, with Russia’s war against Ukraine making the challenge more difficult.

The proposals aim to create mechanisms for regular communication, greater predictability and reducing the risk of future military confrontation.

No veto over Ukraine’s sovereign choices

Kushner emphasized that any future agreement must respect national sovereignty, territorial integrity and countries’ right to determine their own security arrangements.

“Each country will retain authority over its own security and alliances, and no country would have a veto over another’s sovereign choices,” he wrote.

The provision is particularly significant for Ukraine, whose ambitions to join NATO have long been opposed by Moscow.

Kushner also stressed that NATO would remain central to Europe’s collective defense and that the proposed framework would build on existing institutions rather than replace them.

The position contrasts with Russia’s longstanding demands that Ukraine abandon NATO membership ambitions and accept restrictions on its future security arrangements.

Russia to join broader discussions

Kushner said consultations would continue through the Shell Bay format, involving Ukraine, NATO, the EU and European partners.

“We will also engage Russia as part of the peace negotiations,” he wrote.

The announcement comes ahead of US-mediated trilateral talks scheduled for Nov. 10-11 in Abu Dhabi.

As Kyiv Post reported, US envoy Steve Witkoff announced the negotiations earlier this week, saying they would address postwar security arrangements, de-escalation, humanitarian measures and steps toward ending the war.

Kushner said Washington would consult European governments throughout the process, with the possibility of expanding negotiations into a broader multilateral format if progress is achieved.

The proposed security framework remains under discussion, and no agreement has been announced.

Kyiv demands binding security guarantees

The announcement follows a 90-minute conversation Wednesday between President Volodymyr Zelensky and US envoys Kushner and Witkoff.

As Kyiv Post reported, Zelensky said Ukraine had submitted its proposals to Washington and insisted that any postwar security guarantees must be binding and enforceable.

He also pressed the US for additional Patriot missile interceptors as Russia continues striking Ukrainian cities and energy infrastructure.

Kushner acknowledged that the broader negotiations remain difficult but said Washington would continue working toward a comprehensive settlement.

“Creating the right structure will be critical to ending this war and transitioning from conflict toward conditions that make possible a durable peace,” he wrote.

It remains unclear how the proposed framework would accommodate Russia’s demands while upholding Ukraine’s sovereignty, territorial integrity and right to choose its own alliances.
news.summary: US presidential adviser Jared Kushner outlined five objectives for a new European security framework ahead of trilateral peace negotiations with Ukraine and Russia in Abu Dhabi next week. The proposal emphasizes crisis communications, military transparency, de-escalation and national sovereignty, while preserving NATO’s central role in European defense.
news.author: Kyiv Post

news.title: Democrats' election wins spooks AI investors, hammering stocks
news.text: p>Washington: Democrats' sweeping midterm election victory unleashed a rout of tech stocks on Thursday, with investors worried the party will use its gains in state capitols and the US Congress to impose new regulations that will slow the AI infrastructure buildout that has fueled this year's market gains.Two days after Democrats flipped seven seats in the Senate, gained at least 39 in the House of Representatives and picked up five governorships, stocks sold off across the board, with the tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite notching a 5.56 per cent drop, its most dramatic fall in 19 months.The election reflected broad dissatisfaction across America with President Donald Trump, particularly his launching of a war in Iran that has sent fuel costs soaring, powering Democratic wins in Republican-led states including Texas, South Carolina, Kansas and Iowa."Investors appear to be recognizing that some newly elected members of Congress and governors are looking to slow the pace of AI infrastructure development," said Melissa Brown, global head of investment decision research at SimCorp. "While it seems unlikely that they will be able to stop it altogether, any slowdown would raise concerns because the AI growth story has largely depended on the rapid buildout of supporting infrastructure.".Democrats vow to rein in Trump as he shows off White House ballroom.Texas governor-elect Gina Hinojosa, who defeated three-term Republican Greg Abbott, has pledged to halt new data center construction in one of the fastest-growing markets for such AI server farms.Democrats in Congress have also called for new legislation to shield consumers from higher electricity costs tied to data centers and to require independent testing of AI systems.The party's wins promised to give new power to opponents of new data centers, which are at the heart of the AI boom but are loud, thirsty for water, hungry for electricity and increasingly unpopular with their neighbors.Trump's office infrastructure The Republican president, meanwhile, devoted his one public appearance of the day to signing a document aimed at making the White House's Oval Office -- which he has decorated with gold-colored trim and new statues and paintings since returning to power last year -- a national monument."We've had a lot of victories in this office," Trump told reporters, two days after voters handed his fellow Republicans a stunning midterm election defeat. He made no mention of the stock market selloff or the prospect of tougher AI regulation."There's been some mistakes too, but we've had tremendous victory in this office," Trump continued, sitting at a desk now decorated with a red hat bearing the word "VETO" in all capital letters. "So we're making it a national monument, and it will not be allowed to be touched by anybody, destroyed, ripped down by stupid people, in order to build something in a slightly different shape.".Democrats gain influence over trade agenda, but tariff repeals to hit Trump veto wall.Trump had devoted his last pre-election public appearance on Monday to talking about his renovations of the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool, and on Wednesday called in reporters to show off the ballroom he is building at the White House, replacing the historic East Wing that he had demolished.Waiting on Mississippi, Alaska Close Senate races in Alaska and Mississippi - where Democrats hold narrow leads - remained uncalled as of Thursday, leaving open the possibility that the Democrats' majority could increase by two more seats to 56-44.Once seated in January, Democrats are expected to use their power to investigate Trump's administration, family and allies and demand concessions on major legislation.
