news.title: AI rout prompts KOSPI to tumble below 5,000 after US midterm elections
news.text: Digital Desk | Seoul, Nov 6 (IANS) South Korea's benchmark Korea Composite Stock Price Index (KOSPI) sank below 5,000 points on Friday, hit by fears that a Democratic Party victory in the U.S. midterm elections could slow the pace of data centre construction for artificial intelligence (AI). Taking a cue from a tech sell-off on Wall Street overnight, the KOSPI plummeted more than 8 percent, prompting trading on the market to be halted for 20 minutes, reports Yonhap news agency. It was the first time in 16 trading sessions that the KOSPI's 20-minute trading halt was activated. Shares of Samsung Electronics and SK hynix, which account for nearly half of the KOSPI market, plunged more than 10 percent in morning trading. With Democrats winning majorities in both the U.S. Senate and House of Representatives, analysts have predicted that the power of U.S. President Donald Trump will be weakened during the final two years of his term. One of the key things to watch going forward is whether a Democrat-controlled Congress slows the pace of building data centers for artificial intelligence. As the Democratic Party won the gubernatorial leadership in Texas, a key U.S. state in pushing for AI data centres, the tech-heavy NASDAQ slumped more than 5 percent overnight. Some analysts expected volatility to remain elevated in the local stock market. Han Ji-young, an analyst at Kiwoom Securities, said that volatility in the local stock market is likely to continue after the sharp decline. The fear gauge of South Korea's stock market has also jumped as Wall Street's tech sell-off hurt global markets. The KOSPI 200 volatility index (VKOSPI) rose to a three-month high of 64.74 on Friday, according to the Korea Exchange. In a research note, Daishin Securities said the market's reaction to the AI-driven rout was excessive. Lee Kyung-min, an analyst at Daishin Securities, said that the Democratic Party's win may have prompted delays in the construction of AI data centers, but the likelihood of full-scale suspension of such build-out was low. Finance Minister Lee Hyoung-il has vowed to take steps to cope with the excessive volatility in the local stock market. Lee told a meeting with relevant ministers earlier in the day that the government "will preemptively set up measures and take them to prevent our stock markets from excessively responding" to the U.S. tech sell-off. The finance minister said that South Korea will closely monitor external uncertainties but noted that the nation's economic fundamentals remain solid.

news.title: US voters lashed out at data centres. What does that mean for Australia’s AI ambitions?
news.text:
This week’s mid-term elections in the United States saw huge swings to the Democrats, away from President Donald Trump’s Republican party. 

One surprisingly important factor was a rising backlash to the ongoing boom in data centre development triggered by the rise of artificial intelligence (AI) in recent years.

Americans across ten states overwhelmingly voted in favour of candidates campaigning for local restrictions on data centres. 

According to exit polls, some 56% of voters said AI data centres were a crucial or major factor in their vote.

The data centre push

The results are a sign of growing tension between America’s ambition to lead in AI and the willingness of local communities to host the infrastructure needed to support it.

The Trump administration has touted data centre expansion as a core pillar of American technological leadership and economic growth. In July 2025, President Trump signed an executive order to accelerate the development of data centres. 

He has also warned that communities opposing them risk becoming “backwards and poor”.

In June alone, US$4.4 billion was spent on building data centres. This is a fivefold increase from November 2022, when ChatGPT was first released. Around 75% of data centres under construction are currently concentrated in Republican-led states.

However, signs of growing opposition to data centres were clear in the run-up to the midterms.

The data centre backlash

Pew Research showed American sentiment hardening against data centres between January and August this year. Most Americans believe data centres do more harm than good, citing concerns about energy costs, environmental pressures and noise.

Local communities have been especially sensitive to rising home energy prices during an affordability crisis. In areas located near US data centres, wholesale electricity prices have increased by up to 267% over the past five years.

Beyond these impacts to the hip pocket, opposition to data centres also reflects wider public unease about AI. Communities are asking what they stand to gain from AI if they are being asked to foot the bill.

The political cost

Many of the Republican states that Trump won in 2024 encouraged data centres through faster permitting, land use approvals and sweetheart tax deals. But as public opposition grew, candidates from both parties pivoted towards advocating for stronger data centre regulations.

Democrats are more likely than Republicans to view the impacts of data centres negatively. Democratic candidates were quicker to capitalise on the discontent and campaign for tighter oversight and restrictions. Democrat-led states including New Jersey, Michigan, Pennsylvania and Oregon have already introduced local bans or are debating statewide bans.

Republicans were slower to shift, facing tensions between local opposition and President Trump’s support for data centre development.

The 2026 midterms rewarded candidates who campaigned on a platform of restricting data centre buildouts. Gubernatorial races in Texas, Ohio and Georgia – all major growth areas for data centres – were won by candidates calling for pauses on new data centres. 

As the Democratic sweep became apparent, US-based data centre stocks tumbled. States led by Democrats who support restrictions on data centre development account for around 45% of planned US capacity. 

Tighter regulations could mean more project delays and increased costs. Investment may shift towards other jurisdictions or countries with more accommodating regulatory environments.

With the 2028 presidential election approaching, data centres and AI will likely become key battlegrounds. Lawmakers will be mindful of balancing global AI leadership against the mounting local costs of supporting AI compute.

Implications for Australia

Australia’s data centre market is significantly smaller than the US market, but it is growing fast. The backlash is growing, too. 

In September, an A$1.2 billion data centre project in Sydney’s north shore was scrapped in the face of strong community opposition. In Melbourne, residents have used bins and cars to block the construction of huge power lines for a data centre project in West Footscray. 

Australian data centre operator Firmus cancelled a planned stock market listing when interest from overseas investors faded. The company’s signature data centre projects in Tasmania face stiff local opposition.

The Australian government is developing mandatory national standards for large data centres. These will include requirements on energy and water use, project siting and community engagement. Restrictions on developments near homes and recreational facilities have also been flagged. 

However, it is unclear how stringent the requirements will be and how they will interact with existing state and territory rules.

To be effective, the standards will need to address community concerns rather than simply add another layer of regulation and bureaucracy. Clear siting requirements, transparent reporting of resource use, stronger renewable energy commitments, and meaningful early consultation will be essential to winning community approval.

The US midterms demonstrated how data centres can become a potent political issue. If Australia wants to capture the opportunities of AI, it must also earn the trust of the communities expected to host the infrastructure.
news.summary: Community pushback against data centre developments is starting to have big political effects.
news.author: Director,Johanna Lim,Research Associate,Strategic Technologies,United States Studies Centre,University of Sydney,University of Sydney; Olivia Shen

news.title: Elon Musk Spent Big on the Midterms. His Texas Neighbors Voted Differently
news.text: Home to the centerpiece of Elon Musk's Texas empire, Cameron County delivered overwhelming victories to Democratic candidates in 2026 despite the billionaire's record-breaking political spending on Republican causes. The result highlights a striking tension: One of the region's most transformed by Musk's economic investments also became one of the strongest supporters of candidates who openly challenged his political influence. But Cameron County is not just the home of SpaceX's Starbase launch facility near Boca Chica. It is also the home county of Democrat Gina Hinojosa, a Brownsville native who spent much of her campaign attacking what she characterized as Republican Governor Greg Abbott's close relationship with Musk. Brownsville Mayor John Cowen Jr. called Hinojosa's election victory over Abbott a "proud moment" for the city and said he looked forward to working with her administration. Hinojosa vowed Thursday to work with Musk in Texas. "We can have a strong working relationship with Elon Musk and his companies, but it has to be on our terms. We have always been a pro-business state, but data centers have moved into mostly rural communities and there are no rules to protect Texans, so the difference is we will have laws to protect Texans. We can have a strong economy and strong industry, and protections for Texans," Hinojosa told CNN. Newsweek reached out to Hinojosa's campaign and SpaceX for comment. How SpaceX’s Home County Voted in the 2026 Midterms In Texas' marquee races, voters in Cameron County backed James Talarico over Republican Attorney General Ken Paxton by 68 percent to 30 percent. Hinojosa trounced Abbott in the county, 67 percent to 32 percent. In 2024, President Donald Trump carried Cameron County with 52.5 percent of the vote. Democratic Congressman Vicente Gonzalez narrowly defeated Republican Mayra Flores in one of South Texas' most closely watched contests. Two years later, Democrats dominated the county. Gonzalez won reelection with 62 percent of the vote, while Democrats swept major statewide contests, including governor, Senate, lieutenant governor and attorney general. At an early-voting rally, Hinojosa framed the election as a choice between billionaire influence and ordinary Texans. "Is this going to be a Texas that is by and for the people, or is this the billionaires' world and we just live here?" she asked the crowd. She accused Abbott of giving Musk "the keys to the castle" and pointed to disputes involving Boca Chica Beach, communications between Musk's companies and the governor's office, tax incentives and state economic-development decisions. Hinojosa argued that rising costs and declining public services reflected what she called a "Greg Abbott corruption tax," linking those concerns to the state's relationship with major corporate interests, including Musk. Rather than treating Musk solely as a donor, Democrats sought to make him a symbol of concentrated wealth and political influence. That argument was particularly potent in Cameron County, where residents experience both the economic benefits and local impacts of SpaceX's expansion. How Elon Musk Spent His Money in the 2026 Midterms The Tesla and SpaceX chief executive spent more than $445 million backing Republican candidates and causes, including about $225 million in Texas races. Much of that spending was directed toward helping Paxton and supporting Republican turnout efforts. The Texas Senate race was the primary focus of Musk's support. Following the election, Musk responded on X: "guess my election-interfering space lasers didn't work this time." Analysts have also suggested Musk's growing profile may have become a political liability for some Republicans. Speaking on Houston Public Media's Hello Houston after the election, University of Houston professor Brandon Rottinghaus said Musk's visibility had put him "on the ballot in a way" that was difficult for some voters to accept and argued that his presence "magnified" concerns about billionaire influence in politics. Joshua Blank, research director of the Texas Politics Project, said on the same show that Musk's extensive business ties to Texas mean he is likely to remain a major force in the state regardless of who occupies the governor's office. If Democratic control ultimately drives major employers from Texas, Blank said, it would quickly become a political issue in future elections. Where Is SpaceX’s Headquarters? Few communities have benefited more visibly from Musk's arrival than Cameron County. Since SpaceX began developing Boca Chica into Starbase, the company has transformed a once-remote stretch of the Texas coast into one of the world's most closely watched aerospace hubs. Company figures released in recent years said Starbase employed about 4,000 workers and contractors and spent tens of millions of dollars with suppliers throughout the Rio Grande Valley. Local officials have repeatedly highlighted the jobs, investment and economic activity generated by the project. A 2025 local-impact report prepared by the company and released by Cameron County officials projected that SpaceX operations would generate more than $13 billion in gross economic output through 2026. Eddie Treviño Jr., Cameron County judge, has credited the company with helping transform the regional economy through high-skill jobs and infrastructure investment, saying in 2025 that SpaceX's commitment to the county had "transformed our local economy." The 400,000-resident county remains overwhelmingly Hispanic and has historically experienced lower incomes and slower economic growth than many other parts of Texas. Supporters argue SpaceX helped diversify the local economy and create high-paying technical jobs. Abbott frequently made that case during the campaign. "When you look at all the new jobs, not just added by Elon Musk, but look at all the new jobs added by these employers that are coming; those are high-paying jobs," Abbott said during a Rio Grande Valley campaign stop, citing SpaceX among the companies investing in South Texas. Newsweek’s reporters and editors used Martyn, our AI assistant, to produce this story. Learn more about Martyn here. Contact Newsweek editors on this story: Edward T. Cummins
news.summary: Cameron County, home to SpaceX's launch site, overwhelmingly backed Democrats despite Elon Musk's spending on Texas Republicans.
news.author: Jennifer Radcliffe

news.title: Commission Approves Trump’s Triumphal Arch
news.text:
A commission approved on Nov. 5 President Donald Trump’s proposed triumphal arch near the District of Columbia, moving the project closer to reality despite legal challenges.

The National Capital Planning Commission, which is the federal government’s planning agency for the Washington area and consists mostly of people appointed by Trump, gave the green light for the structure. Construction could begin as soon as Friday. But the proposal has sparked three lawsuits, which have been combined into one case.

The plaintiffs have asked U.S. District Judge Tanya Chutkan to prevent construction as long as there is litigation pending. She could rule as soon as Thursday.

One of the parties that have sued is a group of veterans and a historian, represented by public interest law firm Public Citizen Litigation Group. They filed a federal lawsuit seeking to block construction, arguing that the arch would interfere with the historic sightline between the Lincoln Memorial and Arlington House, among other concerns.

She also ordered the administration to provide notice within 30 minutes of any activity related to or in preparation for the construction of the arch.

Chutkan reminded the defendants that any construction or demolition in preparation for construction before the National Park Service issues final agency action authorizing construction or without 14 days’ notice would be a violation of her previous orders.

The administration notified the court on Wednesday that a construction company had an application for a special-use permit to bring equipment and prepare a staging area ahead of construction. The permit had not been issued yet, according to the filing.

The arch has received approval from the Federal Aviation Administration, which was needed due to its proximity to flight paths.

The FAA said in June that the arch would ​need red safety lights, but it does not pose any risk ‌to air traffic at nearby Ronald Reagan Washington National Airport.

The proposed monument would include a mezzanine level at 166 feet, a 24-foot-high observation deck, and a 60-foot statue of Lady Liberty on the top. The structure, which is intended to mark America’s 250th anniversary, would prominently display the inscriptions “One Nation Under God” and “Liberty and Justice for All.” It was inspired by the 164-foot-high Arc de Triomphe in Paris.

The arch is proposed to be built on a man-made island overseen by the National Park Service, located on the Virginia side of the Potomac River near Memorial Bridge, which connects to the Lincoln Memorial. At 250 feet, the structure would be significantly taller than the Lincoln Memorial, which is 99 feet tall, and roughly half the height of the Washington Monument.

The U.S. Commission of Fine Arts voted unanimously on April 16 to move the proposal forward. The commissioners—each appointed by Trump—will review a revised version of the design before making a final decision at a later meeting.

According to former White House press secretary Karoline Leavitt, the height is intended to commemorate the nation’s 250th anniversary. She described the project as an “architectural masterpiece” meant to celebrate American history and foster patriotism across political lines.

“Great nations build beautiful structures that cultivate national pride and love of country, and this triumphal arch should be a project that all Americans, all political persuasions, can support,” she said.

Trump first announced the arch in October 2025.

The proposed arch would create an additional permanent landmark in a city already defined by its monuments. It also builds on his agenda to revitalize and beautify Washington by replacing what he described as “tired” grass, damaged signage, and worn street medians.
news.summary: The proposal has sparked three lawsuits, which have been combined into one case.
news.author: Jackson Richman

news.title: Trump's 250-foot triumphal arch wins approval despite lawsuits and safety concerns
news.text: President Donald Trump's proposed 250-foot (76-meter) triumphal arch in Washington cleared a major regulatory hurdle Thursday night, bringing construction of the towering monument closer to reality despite legal challenges and warnings about traffic congestion, airport safety and public security. The structure, envisioned as a landmark taller than Paris' Arc de Triomphe, is the latest project in Trump's sweeping effort to reshape the U.S. capital. The National Capital Planning Commission voted to approve the proposal after hearing objections from approximately 100 opponents, including Democratic lawmakers. Representative Don Beyer, whose district includes northern Virginia, warned that the project would create lasting problems for the surrounding area. "It will snarl traffic for years, impact the nearby airport, and present even more serious threats to public safety that this commission has refused to acknowledge and grapple with," Beyer said. Despite the approval, construction is not guaranteed. A federal judge considering several legal challenges could still prevent work from beginning. According to the Justice Department, if the project receives final authorization, an initial construction phase lasting six to eight months, focused on excavation and foundation work, could begin as early as this week. Construction above ground would not begin before May 2027, and the entire project is expected to take between 33 and 39 months. In a court filing, the federal government also indicated that the National Park Service could issue a permit or other authorization Thursday, potentially allowing construction to begin this week. A monument taller than Paris' Arc de Triomphe The proposed arch would stand on a highway roundabout near the entrance to Arlington National Cemetery, across the Potomac River from the Lincoln Memorial. At 250 feet tall, it would rise more than 80 feet above the Arc de Triomphe in Paris and approach the height of the U.S. Capitol, which stands at 288 feet (88 meters). The monument's design includes an eternal flame and powerful floodlights intended to make the structure visible to approaching aircraft. A rendering shows the flame supported by a 60-foot (18-meter) golden, winged female figure standing atop the arch, flanked by golden flying eagles. The location has become a particular point of contention because it lies near the final approach route for aircraft landing at Ronald Reagan Washington National Airport. Opponents have raised concerns about the potential impact of such a large structure on aviation and public safety. Trump, however, has emphasized both the monument's appearance and its proposed security functions. Speaking Monday at an event highlighting improvements to the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool, he said the structure could also serve as a military asset, with space to accommodate drones and snipers. "It's right smack in the middle of everything, so very important for our military. But from a beautification standpoint, it'll be the most beautiful arch in the world," Trump said. Legal battle could still halt construction The arch is one of several ambitious and costly construction projects Trump is pursuing in Washington despite opposition from local officials and historic preservation advocates. Other initiatives include rebuilding the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool, constructing a massive White House ballroom and overhauling the Kennedy Center for the Performing Arts. The monument has already become the subject of a significant legal dispute. On Saturday, the state of Virginia and the District of Columbia sued the National Park Service and the Department of the Interior in an effort to stop construction. Their lawsuit described the project as "legally indefensible," arguing that Congress had never authorized the arch. The federal government disputes that interpretation, maintaining that Congress effectively approved the monument more than a century ago when it authorized construction of a bridge across the Potomac River. The approval granted Thursday represents an important step toward realizing Trump's vision, but the project's immediate future remains in the hands of the courts. With foundation work potentially beginning within days, a judge could still determine whether the monument moves forward or construction is halted before it begins.
news.summary: Planned near Arlington National Cemetery, the monument would tower over Paris' Arc de Triomphe and feature a golden winged statue, an eternal flame and military capabilities; critics warn of airport safety risks, while lawsuits could still block construction
news.author: Reuters

news.title: Trump signs order preventing future presidents from changing Oval Office
news.text:
US President Donald Trump has signed an executive order that he says will prevent future presidents from making certain changes to the White House Oval Office.

Trump, a former real estate mogul, has drastically altered the look of the president's official office during his second term, most notably with adding many gold features.

"We're making it a national monument, and it will not be allowed to be touched by anybody, destroyed, ripped down by stupid people, in order to build something in a slightly different shape," Trump told reporters on Thursday.

The order comes months after Trump tore down the entirety of the White House East Wing in a project that has faced legal challenges.

The project was also not approved by the US Congress. Construction has continued, with plans to turn the space into a new ballroom. 

American presidents currently have the power to make some changes to the White House but large projects require the permission of Congress.

The executive order, which Trump signed on Thursday, declares the Oval Office to be a national monument, along with some of its surrounding rooms. 

The document also says that it does not "restrict the President's authority to redecorate the monument, select furnishings, or make ordinary operational and security modifications that do not substantially impair the monument's historic structure or architectural character".

"We like the Oval Office, and it's a symbol, like the White House itself. It's a symbol of our country and the greatness of our country," Trump said, adding that world leaders who have visited in recent months have complimented his decorative changes to the room.

Trump said the White House and the Oval Office had been in need of repairs before his changes, calling it "badly damaged". He described broken windows, cracked walls and broken stone. 

Many of the noticeable changes, though, were cosmetic, including a large gold plaque reading "Oval Office" outside the space, paving over the Rose Garden and adding a new helicopter pad.

Trump said the order would "make it impossible for anybody ever to destroy this incredible space".
news.summary: The order comes after Trump made a series of big changes to the decor of the Oval Office and tore down the White House East Wing.
news.author: Max Matza

news.title: 'No impact on India-US ties': Tharoor says Trump retains power on tariffs, Iran war
news.text: NEW DELHI: Congress MP Shashi Tharoor on Friday said the results of the US midterm elections would have little impact on India-US relations, asserting that President Donald Trump retains considerable powers to pursue his foreign policy agenda despite the ruling party's electoral setback.Speaking in Thiruvananthapuram, Tharoor said the US election results would not change Washington's approach towards key issues such as tariffs, sanctions on countries buying Russian oil, the Iran war or the Ukraine conflict."Whether it comes to tariffs, whether it comes to sanctions for buying Russian oil, whether it comes to the Iran war itself, whether it comes to any initiative he takes on the Ukraine war. All of this, he's completely unaffected by the election result," Tharoor said.He explained that while Congress has significant powers over budgetary matters and can restrict or approve government spending, the President enjoys considerable discretion in foreign policy and international affairs.Tharoor said that even when it comes to military action, the President can proceed without seeking approval for an initial period of up to 60 days. However, Congress can exercise its financial powers to restrict expenditure, particularly in the case of an expensive military campaign."Those in India who are expecting this to have some impact on our relationship with the US, I think, are completely mistaken," he said.Commenting on the election outcome, Tharoor described it as an extraordinary setback for the ruling party, pointing out that midterm elections traditionally serve as a course correction for the party in power.He also highlighted the gains made by candidates from minority communities and people of Indian origin, including the election of a mayor of Indian origin in Los Angeles.Tharoor said the results reflected the vibrancy of American democracy but maintained that the outcome would not significantly alter Trump's ability to take decisions on international affairs.Get the latest India News and Live updates. Elections guru Nate Silver predicted Donald Trump might quit before his term runs out with the Democrats having swept into power for his final two years in office.
The former ABC contributor accurately predicted a 'blue tsunami' ahead of the Tuesday elections, which saw the Democrats win at least 54 Senate seats and 250 House seats, with some contests still to be determined.
On his podcast, Still Counting, he laid out an environment where Trump might retire with time left to serve.
'I had just a weird intuition that maybe Trump will find some pretense to quit, you know what I mean? Because he could get very, very, very isolated, and that also could make him dangerous,' Silver said. 
Silver said that while Trump is not 'evil,' he did give the Republicans a bargain that he now can no longer deliver on. 
'I just think that Republicans made — I was searching for a more original metaphor — but a deal with the devil in Trump, right? And I don’t mean that to mean that he’s evil. I mean that in the sense of, like, you get your three Supreme Court justices, you get tax breaks for the wealthy, but you pay a lot of f***ing price for that,' he said.
Silver also accused Trump of having 'sucked out the oxygen from anybody else in the Republican Party.'
He also thinks that Trump might step aside to allow JD Vance to assume incumbency status.

news.title: Trump makes the Oval Office a national monument. But future presidents can still redecorate
news.text: WASHINGTON, D.C. — President Donald Trump on Thursday signed a proclamation that he says will preserve the Oval Office and Cabinet Room as a national monument, his first official action after his party was swept aside in midterm elections on Tuesday.But the action does not prevent future presidents from restyling the iconic office that Trump has filled to the brim with gold flourishes, nor does it prevent a successor from rolling back the proclamation itself. Trump himself has reversed national monument designations made by his predecessors.Trump, however, described the Oval Office order in expansive terms. “It will not be allowed to be touched by anybody, destroyed, ripped down by stupid people, in order to build something in a slightly different shape,” Trump said. “We like the Oval Office, and it’s a symbol, like the White House itself.”It was the third day this week that the president, a real estate mogul, delivered remarks fixated on his pet projects in Washington. On Wednesday, a day after Republicans suffered defeats in key races across the country, Trump gathered reporters to sign the final beam being raised during construction of his opulent ballroom project. On Monday, he went to the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool to talk about his renovation of the landmark.The proclamation, released after Trump's remarks, says that nothing in it will “restrict the President’s authority to redecorate the monument, select furnishings, or make ordinary operational and security modifications that do not substantially impair the monument’s historic structure or architectural character.”It orders the Interior secretary to manage the Oval Office and requires “documentation, review, and consideration of alternatives before any action that would substantially alter or demolish the monument.” Trump separately said any major changes would need review from Congress, though such a requirement is not in the document's text.“If they want to say, ‘Let’s not have oval anymore, let’s make it square,’ what happens is they have to go back to Congress and hopefully the Congress, the people in Congress, will be smart enough not to let that happen,” said Trump — who notably demolished the East Wing of the White House to make room for his ballroom.A red baseball cap with “VETO” on the front was sitting on the Resolute Desk as Trump signed the document, a not-so-subtle nod to the shifting of powers in Congress.His effort to preserve changes at the White House comes as Democrats gear up for new scrutiny of Trump. Connecticut Sen. Richard Blumenthal, the top Democrat on the Homeland Security Committee’s Permanent Subcommittee on Investigations, sent a flurry of letters Thursday to known donors to Trump’s ballroom, demanding that they provide information or face “alternative measures to obtain compliance.”Since returning to the White House, Trump has overseen numerous design changes to various rooms, including the Oval Office, where he has filled the wall space with portraits, a copy of the Declaration of Independence and numerous golden accents.As he talked about his interior decorating decisions, Trump highlighted new chandeliers that he says were installed in the Cabinet Room to address “very bad lighting.” His other additions to the Oval Office include numerous gold wall appliqués and gold-framed portraits.Trump did not elaborate on precisely what he was hoping to prevent but suggested that the Oval Office might face some threat in the future. Trump himself has faced several lawsuits alleging that his Washington beautification projects were done without the necessary approval.“If anybody ever decides to come and start knocking down walls, you call me wherever I may be,' Trump said, “and I’ll come back here and I’ll make sure it never happens.”

news.title: Iran strike still on the table as IDF awaits Washington's next move
news.text: Even after the elections in Israel and the United States, the possibility of a strike on Iran remains an open question. At this stage, there have been no dramatic developments in the buildup of U.S. forces in the region, apart from the reinforcement of American forces in southern Israel and several movements in the Arabian Sea that are not particularly unusual. No significant signs of increased preparations have been detected so far. However, defense officials emphasize that the situation could change rapidly, depending on decisions made in Washington and the objectives of any potential operation. The IDF, meanwhile, continues its routine operational activities without any unusual developments, awaiting diplomatic developments to determine which direction events may take. Before Israel's elections, significant tensions emerged between IDF Chief of Staff Lt. Gen. Eyal Zamir and Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and Defense Minister Israel Katz over the latter two's desire to advance a particular operation in Iran. Zamir, who expressed concern that Israel's elections could be canceled if a major operation against Iran were launched, blocked the move together with the Americans. Another confrontation arose over the military operation in Hebron, launched following a deadly terrorist attack that killed two IDF soldiers approximately two weeks ago. During the election period, the IDF's senior leadership exercised particular caution in its dealings with the political leadership and the public, almost entirely suspending briefings and background discussions in an effort to keep the military out of the political arena. Even now, after the elections have ended, concerns remain about major operations, particularly against Iran, that could result in damage to Israel's home front and affect the political developments currently unfolding. Regarding Iran, Israeli defense officials are seeking to understand not only whether fighting will resume, but also what its objectives would be. Israel and the United States previously launched Operation Roaring Lion with a shared interest in weakening the Iranian regime. Now, however, their objectives do not necessarily appear to align. Netanyahu speaks of toppling the regime, while voices in the United States advocate an intense, swift military operation that would weaken Iran and bring it to the negotiating table from a position of disadvantage, with the aim of securing a better nuclear agreement. Such an agreement could be presented as an achievement for President Donald Trump following his party's poor performance in the midterm elections. At the same time, the IDF is refining its procedures and maintaining readiness for the possibility of a major operation against Iran. Military planning also takes into account the possibility that such an operation could involve another round of fighting in Lebanon. Forces along the Lebanese border continue operations to clear the area, although a significant portion of their efforts is now focused on preparing positions and adapting operational procedures for winter. The IDF is also preparing strike plans against Hezbollah in southern Lebanon should they become necessary. In the West Bank, the IDF is working to keep tensions below the threshold of escalation. At this stage, as of the time of writing, the military has managed to some extent to interrupt the sequence of terrorist attacks carried out by individuals and local cells. Recent weeks have seen an increase in the pace of settlement establishment, particularly in Samaria and the Binyamin region of the West Bank. The assessment is that this trend could accelerate if government officials believe the bloc seeking to replace Netanyahu is approaching the formation of a new government, or if a caretaker government remains in place ahead of another election. A senior security official said: "The trends in nationalist crime remain extremely negative. The phenomenon is growing, and we are not seeing anything positive in the handling of these incidents. With the political developments, it will intensify even further, and the scale of nationalist crime will continue to increase. The pace of people moving into settlements and the establishment of outposts has risen significantly, and this is placing an extreme strain on the IDF."
news.summary: With no major US military buildup detected, the IDF is maintaining readiness for renewed fighting with Iran, as Israel and Washington weigh differing objectives and military planners consider the possibility of another round of fighting in Lebanon

news.title: Japan’s Nikkei plunges 5.7%, South Korea’s Kospi falls 7.4% amid AI stock rout
news.text: Tokyo Japan’s stock benchmark tumbled more than 6 per cent after trading opened Friday, and other Asian stocks also declined following a widespread sell-off of issues related to artificial intelligence on Wall Street. Tokyo’s benchmark Nikkei 225 recouped some of those initial losses, trading 5.7 per cent lower at 57,576.63 by midday. Australia’s S&P/ASX 200 lost 1.0 per cent to 8,973.00. South Korea’s Kospi dropped 7.4 per cent to 4,985.99, as Samsung Electronics shares shed 7.9% in morning trading. Hong Kong’s Hang Seng fell 0.7 per cent to 24,630.03, while the Shanghai Composite dipped 1.3 per cent to 3,642.10. Asian markets slide after Wall Street sell-off Stock markets around the world have been feeling pressure from continued declines for companies that have benefited from the boom in the artificial-intelligence technology industry. Such stocks have been swinging for months on worries that the construction of AI data centres may slow because of how expensive it’s become to borrow money. Critics also say AI stock prices had shot too high and were in a bubble. Toyota stock declined sharply after the Japanese automaker reported lackluster profits the previous day. Nintendo, which also reported earnings the previous day, saw its stock price fall amid the overall market tumble. Sony Group stock fell slightly. The company reported booming results on the back of the success of its latest Spider-Man movie. S&P 500 posts biggest daily fall since April 2025 On Wall Street, the S&P 500 fell 4.4 per cent Thursday for its worst day since US President Donald Trump shook markets worldwide in April 2025 with his “Liberation Day” tariffs. The wipeout more than erased the US stock market’s gain from the day before, which was its best in three months. The Dow Jones Industrial Average sank 1,833 points, or 3.4 per cent, while the Nasdaq composite tumbled 5.5 per cent. The Nasdaq, which is full of AI-related and other tech stocks, sank 11.9 per cent below its all-time high set last month. Stock geeks call a loss of more than 10 per cent a “correction.” US midterm election results add to AI sector concerns Tuesday’s US midterm elections added another challenge. The nationwide victories for Democrats raised the possibility that governments could force pauses in construction of more data centres. Voters across political parties say they’re wary about AI and don’t like the increases to power bills caused by data centers. Any slowdown in construction of AI data centres would mean fewer purchases of AI chips, not to mention electricity and other products and services that are getting vacuumed up in the AI frenzy, which is driving much of the US economy’s growth. Nvidia and other AI-linked stocks lead market losses Nvidia, the chip company that quickly became the face of the AI boom, fell 9.3 per cent and was by far the heaviest weight on the S&P 500. It’s now down 2.6 per cent for the year so far following annual gains of roughly 39 per cent, 171 per cent and 239 per cent in the last three years. Advanced Micro Devices tumbled 17.3 per cent. CoreWeave, a company that rents access to AI chips to customers over the cloud, fell 9.8 per cent. GE Vernova, which has been helping to power data centers, sank 7.5 per cent. Compounding the pain for investors, AI chip stocks are some of Wall Street’s most influential because they’ve become some of the largest. A 1 per cent move for Nvidia, for example, has more effect on the S&P 500 than a 1 per cent move for nearly any other US stock. Stock prices tend to follow where corporate profits and interest rates go over the long term, depending on them much more than on who controls what in Washington. US markets close sharply lower; oil prices rise All told, the S&P 500 fell 334.89 points to 7,353.73. The Dow Jones Industrial Average dropped 1,833.06 to 51,523.06, and the Nasdaq composite sank 1,421.52 to 24,315.00. In energy trading, benchmark US crude added 0.65 per cent to USD 91.11 a barrel. Brent crude, the international standard, gained 1.4 per cent to USD 99.73 a barrel. Uncertainty still reigns about what will happen in the war with Iran and when the global energy industry can return to normal. Treasury yields fall as investors seek safer assets In the bond market, Treasury yields continued to tumble Thursday. The yield on the 10-year Treasury fell to 4.84 per cent from 4.90 per cent late Wednesday. It had been at 4.95 per cent on election night and above 5.30 per cent last month. That could be a signal that investors are herding into US Treasury bonds in search of something that’s safer to own as stock prices tumble. The drop in yields came despite some encouraging reports on the US economy. Fewer US workers applied for unemployment benefits last week. In currency trading, the US dollar rose to 157.97 Japanese yen from 157.68 yen. The euro cost USD 1.1209, down from USD1.1219.
news.summary: Concerns over expensive AI infrastructure, stretched technology valuations and potential data centre construction delays have intensified selling pressure across global equity markets

news.title: Marco Rubio denies exit plans, vows to serve Trump’s full second term
news.text:
Washington, DC: US Secretary of State Marco Rubio has dismissed reports suggesting that he is considering leaving the Trump administration following the Republican Party’s setbacks in the midterm elections, insisting that completing President Donald Trump’s second term has always been his plan.
In an interview with The New York Times, Rubio rejected speculation that he might step down to prepare for a 2028 presidential campaign, clarifying his long-term professional intentions within the executive branch.
“Working for President Trump for the duration of his second term has always been my plan,” Rubio said.
“I don’t know where these things come from, to be honest with you,” he added, addressing widespread rumours regarding his possible departure.
Addressing queries concerning his diverse portfolio, Rubio downplayed the workload, stating that he enjoys his current duties and maintains a sense of humour about the constant speculation.
Rubio also dismissed questions about his multiple responsibilities in the administration, saying, “I love the work I’m doing. And plus I always laugh when they say he’s going to leave his job. I go, ‘Which one?’”
These narratives began circulating following the Republican Party’s setbacks in the midterm elections, which subsequently sparked fresh speculation regarding future party leadership and prospective presidential contenders for 2028.
In response to the rumours, officials from both the White House and the Department of State firmly refuted the claims.
White House spokesperson Beni Rae Harmony characterised the stories as a fabricated hoax pushed by anonymous sources, emphasising that Rubio remains a committed supporter of Trump and the MAGA movement.
Assistant Secretary of State for Global Public Affairs Dylan Johnson also called the reports completely baseless fake news.
Despite official denials, political analysts increasingly view Rubio as a viable presidential hopeful for 2028, particularly amid growing discussions surrounding Vice President JD Vance’s political standing after the recent midterms.
Even so, insiders cited by The New York Post noted that Rubio’s original framework always involved serving through the entirety of President Trump’s second term.
A high-ranking administration official confirmed that Rubio planned from the outset to serve all four years, humorously noting that he had stated he would not take a holiday.
Presently, Rubio manages two influential positions as Secretary of State and National Security Adviser, placing him centrally within the executive branch’s national security framework and foreign policy planning.
Furthermore, he continues to work closely alongside White House Chief of Staff Susie Wiles and Vice President JD Vance.
Another key factor influencing his tenure is his lifelong dedication to achieving political transformation in Cuba.
As the son of Cuban immigrants, challenging Cuba’s communist government has remained a cornerstone of his political career, making him hesitant to leave office before fulfilling these key foreign policy objectives.
Conservative donor Dan Eberhart noted that the electoral outcome had altered the political landscape for potential future candidates.
“The midterms blew up Vance’s [2028 prospects] and Rubio’s stock is soaring,” Eberhart said.
He observed that returning to Miami might prove difficult for Rubio before he successfully tackles his mission against the Cuban regime.
While Rubio previously remarked that he would step aside if Vice President Vance sought the Republican nomination in 2028, the recent electoral climate has only intensified speculation regarding an alternative bid.
When pressed on his future political ambitions during his interview with The New York Times, Rubio firmly declined to entertain any discussion regarding the 2028 race.
“I literally will not talk about 2028 anymore,” he said. “I just won’t do it.”
Looking ahead, Rubio is scheduled to deliver his first major speech after the midterm elections next Friday at the Federalist Society’s National Lawyers Convention in Washington, DC.

news.title: Hegseth defends record as Pengaton chief, slams 'sham' push for his impeachment
news.text:
U.S. Secretary of War Pete Hegseth issued a video message on Thursday vowing to fight efforts in Congress to impeach him and defending the Iran war as "courageous and historic" after voters punished Republicans over it in this week's midterm elections. 

Hegseth's remarks, posted ‌on social media, came as taunts from his foes in Congress intensified and U.S. President Donald Trump swatted away questions about whether he might fire Hegseth. Trump has commended his Pentagon chief. 

The top Democrat in the House of Representatives, Hakeem Jeffries, asked in a post: "Why is Pete Hegseth still around?" 

Hegseth, a former Fox News host, has been a polarizing figure who has made enemies even within his own Republican Party. Critics in Congress are targeting his conduct ​of the Iran war, which U.S. Vice President JD Vance has said cost Republicans control of Congress, ​his firing of top military officers and strained relations with lawmakers as the administration seeks a $1.5-trillion US defence spending package.

Calls to investigate Hegseth

Democrats, who won control of Congress in Tuesday's elections, have promised to investigate Hegseth and his handling of the Pentagon, and congressional aides say that would include the ​firing of the chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff, among other issues. 

Republican Rep. Thomas Massie promised to reintroduce articles of impeachment ⁠against Hegseth next week, warning that impeachment would ⁠be "much gentler" than what's in store for him once Republicans cede control of Congress next year ‌to Democrats.

"They'll have hearings & trials," Massie wrote on X. 

JD Vance blames Iran war for midterm thumping. Is he really blaming Trump?

Hegseth defended his stewardship of the Pentagon in a more than four-minute video that boasted about firing senior Pentagon leaders, ending diversity initiatives and banning transgender individuals from the military. 

"You see, they attack me — they attack us — because we are effective. It's not going to work. We will not back down," Hegseth said to the camera. 

Impeachment 'didn't work' against Trump: Hegeseth

Calling the impeachment effort a "sham," Hegseth said that Trump himself was impeached ⁠twice. 

"It's all about the politics of personal destruction. It didn't work against President Trump, and it won't work with me. You can rest assured of that," he said. 

Trump on Thursday praised Hegseth when asked whether he expected any staffing changes, saying his defence secretary had "done a fantastic job" and suggesting that the opposition to him was tied to his firing ‌of generals. 

"We had so many generals. Everybody was a four-star general. I never saw anything like it. And many of those people were woke. I don't like a woke general. And so, he probably has opposition," Trump told reporters in the Oval Office. 

Trump also praised Hegseth's role in U.S. military operations in Venezuela and Iran. 

"Venezuela has been unbelievable ... and in Iran, we are there for seven months and we control everything that we've wanted to control," he ​said. 

Could be 'on chopping block'

Sources have said Trump could still replace Hegseth as Republicans assess their election losses.

On Wednesday, Vance publicly questioned whether the Iran war was worth it and said it cost Republicans control of Congress, in extraordinary remarks ⁠that raised questions about whether Trump might still go ahead with a threatened resumption of major combat operations against Iran. 

One Trump adviser said Hegseth "could be on the chopping block" ⁠because of the Iran war.

The War Department has said Hegseth is "100 per cent committed" to leading the Pentagon until the end of Trump's term. 

Hegseth appealed to "patriotic" lawmakers to ⁠pass a ⁠funding request that aims to help the Pentagon pay for the ​Iran war and other spending priorities.

"Regardless of how people feel about the war, which I believe is a courageous and historic effort that will ensure Iran never gets nuclear weapons, ​we need to continue, as President Trump did in ⁠his first term, to rebuild our military," Hegseth said.

Hegseth faces 'a reckoning': senator

Republican Sen. Thom Tillis told CBS news on Tuesday night that Hegseth has "a reckoning" coming and his strained relationship with lawmakers was undermining the Trump administration's push for a $1.5-trillion US defence spending package in Congress.

Hegseth could also face scrutiny from Democrats over his Ukraine policy and U.S. military strikes on suspected drug trafficking boats in Latin American waters, which some Democrats say could amount to war crimes.

Representative Adam Smith, the Democrat who is expected to lead the House Armed Services Committee next year, promised vigorous oversight on everything ⁠from the Iran war to what he called the ‌erosion of the "apolitical foundation of the armed forces."
news.summary: U.S. Secretary of War Pete Hegseth issued a video message on Thursday vowing to fight efforts in Congress to impeach him and defending the Iran war as "courageous and historic" after voters punished Republicans over it in this week’s midterm elections.

news.title: Marco Rubio Denies Exit Plans, Vows to Serve Trump's Full Second Term
news.text: US Secretary of State Marco Rubio has dismissed reports suggesting that he is considering leaving the Trump administration following the Republican Party's setbacks in the midterm elections, insisting that completing President Donald Trump's second term has always been his plan.In an interview with The New York Times, Rubio rejected speculation that he might step down to prepare for a 2028 presidential campaign, clarifying his long-term professional intentions within the executive branch.“Working for President Trump for the duration of his second term has always been my plan,” Rubio said. “I don’t know where these things come from, to be honest with you,” he added, addressing widespread rumours regarding his possible departure.Addressing queries concerning his diverse portfolio, Rubio downplayed the workload, stating that he enjoys his current duties and maintains a sense of humour about the constant speculation.Rubio also dismissed questions about his multiple responsibilities in the administration, saying, “I love the work I’m doing. And plus I always laugh when they say he’s going to leave his job. I go, ‘Which one?’”These narratives began circulating following the Republican Party's setbacks in the midterm elections, which subsequently sparked fresh speculation regarding future party leadership and prospective presidential contenders for 2028.In response to the rumours, officials from both the White House and the Department of State firmly refuted the claims. White House spokesperson Beni Rae Harmony characterised the stories as a fabricated hoax pushed by anonymous sources, emphasising that Rubio remains a committed supporter of Trump and the MAGA movement.Assistant Secretary of State for Global Public Affairs Dylan Johnson also called the reports completely baseless fake news.Despite official denials, political analysts increasingly view Rubio as a viable presidential hopeful for 2028, particularly amid growing discussions surrounding Vice President JD Vance's political standing after the recent midterms.Even so, insiders cited by The New York Post noted that Rubio's original framework always involved serving through the entirety of President Trump's second term.A high-ranking administration official confirmed that Rubio planned from the outset to serve all four years, humorously noting that he had stated he would not take a holiday.Presently, Rubio manages two influential positions as Secretary of State and National Security Adviser, placing him centrally within the executive branch's national security framework and foreign policy planning.Furthermore, he continues to work closely alongside White House Chief of Staff Susie Wiles and Vice President JD Vance.Another key factor influencing his tenure is his lifelong dedication to achieving political transformation in Cuba.As the son of Cuban immigrants, challenging Cuba's communist government has remained a cornerstone of his political career, making him hesitant to leave office before fulfilling these key foreign policy objectives.Conservative donor Dan Eberhart noted that the electoral outcome had altered the political landscape for potential future candidates.“The midterms blew up Vance’s [2028 prospects] and Rubio’s stock is soaring,” Eberhart said.He observed that returning to Miami might prove difficult for Rubio before he successfully tackles his mission against the Cuban regime.While Rubio previously remarked that he would step aside if Vice President Vance sought the Republican nomination in 2028, the recent electoral climate has only intensified speculation regarding an alternative bid.When pressed on his future political ambitions during his interview with The New York Times, Rubio firmly declined to entertain any discussion regarding the 2028 race.“I literally will not talk about 2028 anymore,” he said. “I just won’t do it.”Looking ahead, Rubio is scheduled to deliver his first major speech after the midterm elections next Friday at the Federalist Society's National Lawyers Convention in Washington, DC.

news.title: Asian benchmarks decline after AI worries send Wall Street tumbling
news.text: TOKYO: Japan's stock benchmark tumbled more than 6% after trading opened Friday, and other Asian stocks also declined following a widespread sell-off of issues related to artificial intelligence on Wall Street.Tokyo's benchmark Nikkei 225 recouped some of those initial losses, trading 5.7% lower at 57,576.63 by midday. Australia's S&P/ASX 200 lost 1.0% to 8,973.00. South Korea's Kospi dropped 7.4% to 4,985.99, as Samsung Electronics shares shed 7.9% in morning trading. Hong Kong's Hang Seng fell 0.7% to 24,630.03, while the Shanghai Composite dipped 1.3% to 3,642.10.Stock markets around the world have been feeling pressure from continued declines for companies that have benefited from the boom in the artificial-intelligence technology industry. Such stocks have been swinging for months on worries that the construction of AI data centers may slow because of how expensive it's become to borrow money. Critics also say AI stock prices had shot too high and were in a bubble.Toyota stock declined sharply after the Japanese automaker reported lackluster profits the previous day. Nintendo, which also reported earnings the previous day, saw its stock price fall amid the overall market tumble. Sony Group stock fell slightly. The company reported booming results on the back of the success of its latest Spider-Man movie.On Wall Street, the S&P 500 fell 4.4% Thursday for its worst day since U.S. President Donald Trump shook markets worldwide in April 2025 with his "Liberation Day" tariffs. The wipeout more than erased the U.S. stock market's gain from the day before, which was its best in three months.The Dow Jones Industrial Average sank 1,833 points, or 3.4%, while the Nasdaq composite tumbled 5.5%. The Nasdaq, which is full of AI-related and other tech stocks, sank 11.9% below its all-time high set last month. Stock geeks call a loss of more than 10% a "correction.".Tuesday's U.S. midterm elections added another challenge. The nationwide victories for Democrats raised the possibility that governments could force pauses in construction of more data centers. Voters across political parties say they're wary about AI and don't like the increases to power bills caused by data centers.Any slowdown in construction of AI data centers would mean fewer purchases of AI chips, not to mention electricity and other products and services that are getting vacuumed up in the AI frenzy, which is driving much of the U.S. economy's growth.Nvidia, the chip company that quickly became the face of the AI boom, fell 9.3% and was by far the heaviest weight on the S&P 500. It's now down 2.6% for the year so far following annual gains of roughly 39%, 171% and 239% in the last three years.Advanced Micro Devices tumbled 17.3%. CoreWeave, a company that rents access to AI chips to customers over the cloud, fell 9.8%. GE Vernova, which has been helping to power data centers, sank 7.5%.Compounding the pain for investors, AI chip stocks are some of Wall Street's most influential because they've become some of the largest. A 1% move for Nvidia, for example, has more effect on the S&P 500 than a 1% move for nearly any other U.S. stock.Stock prices tend to follow where corporate profits and interest rates go over the long term, depending on them much more than on who controls what in Washington.All told, the S&P 500 fell 334.89 points to 7,353.73. The Dow Jones Industrial Average dropped 1,833.06 to 51,523.06, and the Nasdaq composite sank 1,421.52 to 24,315.00.In energy trading, benchmark U.S. crude added 0.65% to $91.11 a barrel. Brent crude, the international standard, gained 1.4% to $99.73 a barrel. Uncertainty still reigns about what will happen in the war with Iran and when the global energy industry can return to normal.In the bond market, Treasury yields continued to tumble Thursday. The yield on the 10-year Treasury fell to 4.84% from 4.90% late Wednesday. It had been at 4.95% on election night and above 5.30% last month. That could be a signal that investors are herding into U.S. Treasury bonds in search of something that's safer to own as stock prices tumble.The drop in yields came despite some encouraging reports on the U.S. economy. Fewer U.S. workers applied for unemployment benefits last week.In currency trading, the U.S. dollar rose to 157.97 Japanese yen from 157.68 yen. The euro cost $1.1209, down from $1.1219..Follow The New Indian Express channel on WhatsApp Download the TNIE app to stay with us and follow the latest

news.title: Rupee to draw support from return of foreign flows amid tech meltdown
news.text: MUMBAI The rupee on Friday will draw support from a return of foreign capital ​to Indian markets after months of sustained outflows, with a ‌technology rout offering a tailwind for capital flows ​into Asia's third-largest economy. https://www.thehindubusinessline.com/topic/rupee/ The rupee has ⁠advanced 0.5 per cent so far this week, hitting a two-week high of 94.32 in Thursday's session before settling at 94.4750. It is ‌expected to open largely flat, with a slight positive bias. The Indian currency, which has remained ‌under pressure for much of the year and ‌relied ⁠heavily on central bank intervention for support, has ⁠found relief this week from two factors that had weighed on it for months — oil prices and equity flows. https://www.thehindubusinessline.com/topic/CRUDE_OIL/ Oil prices have ​retreated on expectations that ‌the Republican Party's losses in the US midterm elections could constrain President Donald Trump's political room to sustain the conflict with Iran. Meanwhile, foreign investors have been ‌buying Indian equities, with the retreat from AI-linked technology ​stocks offering a potential boost to markets that had lost out amid capital chasing the ⁠AI trade. The reversal in those trades is now bringing Indian equities back into focus. The technology rout intensified ‌on Thursday after the Democratic Party victory in the US midterm raised concerns about greater regulatory scrutiny and potential curbs on the expansion of AI data centres. The Nasdaq Composite plunged 5.5 per cent, while the Philadelphia Semiconductor Index tumbled more than 12 per cent. Technology-heavy Asian markets came under ‌pressure on Friday. In comparison, losses in Indian equities were expected ​to be relatively contained. Foreign investors bought a net $1.6 billion of Indian equities on Thursday, their biggest ⁠single-day purchase in nearly six years, according to provisional exchange ⁠data. This followed net purchases of about $2.2 billion over the previous four sessions. Whether the return of ‌foreign capital marks a more sustained reversal in investor sentiment towards India will be key for ​the rupee's outlook alongside oil, traders said.
news.summary: The rupee has ⁠advanced 0.5% so far this week, hitting a two-week high of 94.32 in Thursday's session before settling at 94.4750; It is ‌expected to open largely flat, with a slight positive bias

news.title: Trump links stock market decline to US midterm election results
news.text:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, November 6. US President
Donald Trump has linked the decline in major stock markets to the
results of the midterm elections, which could result in Democrats
gaining control of Congress.

The American leader shared his views on the matter in a post on
his Truth Social account.

"The stock market has experienced one of the worst days in its
history due to the election results. It’s very sad to see! It took
a lot of effort to get us to levels never seen before, and now this
has happened," Trump wrote.

It should be noted that the US midterm elections were held on
November 3. Voters elected 35 of the 100 members of the Senate and
all 435 members of the House of Representatives. Gubernatorial
elections were also held in 36 states.

On Wednesday and Thursday, shares of several leading US
companies, as well as companies in a number of other countries,
recorded significant declines.
news.author: Muzaffar Ibrahimov
